p7-l001-temperature-kinetic-ideal-gas.prompt: Why does the zeroth law of thermodynamics make a thermometer possible?
options: It states that energy is conserved, so a thermometer can simply track the energy changes of the sample.
It states that heat flows from hot to cold, so the thermometer always reads the hotter of two objects.
If A and C are each in equilibrium with B, they are in equilibrium with each other.
It guarantees that all objects eventually reach absolute zero, which gives the thermometer its reference point.
p7-l001-temperature-kinetic-ideal-gas.explanation: Transitivity of thermal equilibrium means a single number labels each equilibrium class. A thermometer is any system with a convenient property that varies with that number.

p7-l001-temperature-kinetic-ideal-gas.prompt: Estimate the root-mean-square speed of N$_2$ molecules ($m=28.014$ u) at 300 K from $\tfrac12mv_{rms}^2=\tfrac32kT$. Give the answer in m/s. ($u=1.6605\times10^{-27}$ kg)
p7-l001-temperature-kinetic-ideal-gas.explanation: $v_{rms}=\sqrt{3kT/m}=517$ m/s, comparable to the speed of sound in air (about 340 m/s) -- not a coincidence.

p7-l001-temperature-kinetic-ideal-gas.prompt: In the kinetic-theory derivation of the ideal gas law, what produces the pressure the gas exerts on a wall?
options: Molecules repelling one another and pushing outward on the wall with a steady force.
The average momentum delivered per second by molecules rebounding from the wall.
The weight of the gas above the wall pressing down on it under gravity.
Molecules sticking to the wall briefly and releasing their thermal energy there.
p7-l001-temperature-kinetic-ideal-gas.explanation: Each rebounding molecule transfers momentum $2mv_x$ to the wall; the time-averaged rate of momentum transfer per unit area is the pressure, giving $PV=\tfrac13 Nm\overline{v^2}=NkT$.

p7-l001-temperature-kinetic-ideal-gas.prompt: Explain how kinetic theory connects the temperature of a gas to the motion of its molecules, and why this makes a thermometer reading physically meaningful.
p7-l001-temperature-kinetic-ideal-gas.rubric: Full credit requires: pressure from momentum transfer to the walls; $PV=NkT$ combined with $PV=\tfrac13Nm\overline{v^2}$ gives mean translational kinetic energy $\tfrac32kT$; temperature is therefore a measure of mean molecular kinetic energy, and a thermometer in equilibrium with the gas shares this temperature (zeroth law).
p7-l001-temperature-kinetic-ideal-gas.modelAnswer: Wall collisions give $P=\tfrac13 n m\overline{v^2}$. Comparing with $PV=NkT$ shows the mean translational kinetic energy per molecule is $\tfrac32kT$, so temperature measures molecular kinetic energy. A thermometer in thermal equilibrium with the gas reads that same $T$ by the zeroth law.

p7-l002-equipartition-freeze-out.prompt: A sample of H$_2$ gas at 300 K has a heat capacity $C_V\approx\tfrac52Nk$, not $\tfrac72Nk$ as full equipartition would predict for three translations, two rotations and one vibration (two quadratic terms). Why?
options: The vibrational level spacing greatly exceeds $kT$ at 300 K, so that mode is frozen out.
Hydrogen is monatomic, so only translation matters and rotation or vibration cannot be excited.
Rotation of the molecule is forbidden at room temperature, so only vibration and translation contribute.
Equipartition is always wrong for molecules and only works for single atoms, never for diatomics.
p7-l002-equipartition-freeze-out.explanation: Equipartition applies only when $kT$ is large compared with the spacing between quantum levels of the mode. Vibration of H$_2$ needs about 6000 K to unfreeze; rotation (about 85 K) is already active.

p7-l002-equipartition-freeze-out.prompt: As a sample of H$_2$ gas is cooled from 300 K to about 30 K, its $C_V$ drops from about $\tfrac52Nk$ toward $\tfrac32Nk$. Why?
options: The molecules stop translating at low temperature, so only the internal modes remain active.
The H-H bond breaks as the gas cools, leaving separate atoms that have only translational energy.
The gas liquefies and equipartition no longer applies to liquids, so the heat capacity changes.
Rotational spacings become large compared with $kT$, so rotation freezes out and only translation is left.
p7-l002-equipartition-freeze-out.explanation: Rotational constant for H$_2$ is large (small moment of inertia), so the rotational temperature is about 85 K. Below roughly that, rotation freezes. Heavier molecules unfreeze much earlier.

p7-l002-equipartition-freeze-out.prompt: Estimate the heat needed to raise 1.00 mol of N$_2$ gas by 10.0 K at constant volume near 300 K, using equipartition with translation and rotation active and vibration frozen out. Give the answer in J.
p7-l002-equipartition-freeze-out.explanation: With 3 translational and 2 rotational quadratic terms, $C_V=\tfrac52R$ per mole, so $Q=\tfrac52R\,\Delta T\approx208$ J.

p7-l002-equipartition-freeze-out.prompt: Explain why the heat capacity of a gas of diatomic molecules rises in steps as temperature increases (translation, then rotation, then vibration), in terms of energy-level spacings.
p7-l002-equipartition-freeze-out.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) a mode contributes kT/2 per quadratic term to the energy only when kT is comparable to or greater than the spacing of its quantised levels; (2) translational spacings are tiny, rotational are about 10^-3 to 10^-2 eV (tens of K), vibrational are about 0.1-0.5 eV (thousands of K); (3) so each mode 'switches on' in turn as T increases, producing steps.
p7-l002-equipartition-freeze-out.modelAnswer: A quantised mode can only absorb energy if the thermal energy $kT$ is enough to excite it to its next level. Translational spacings are essentially zero, so translation is always active. Rotational spacings are about $10^{-3}$ eV (tens of kelvin) and vibrational spacings about $0.1$ eV (thousands of kelvin), so rotation turns on at low temperature and vibration at high temperature. Each switch-on adds a step to $C_V$.

p7-l003-first-law-quasistatic-work.prompt: Which statement about internal energy, heat and work is correct?
options: Heat and work are both state functions, just like the internal energy $U$.
$U$ is a state function; heat and work are energy-transfer modes that depend on the path.
Heat is energy stored in a body, whereas work is energy in the process of being transferred.
Work is a state function, whereas heat depends on the path taken between the two states.
p7-l003-first-law-quasistatic-work.explanation: $\Delta U=Q+W$. Different paths between the same states can have different $Q$ and $W$ but always the same $\Delta U$.

p7-l003-first-law-quasistatic-work.prompt: Why is it important that a compression be quasistatic when evaluating $W=-\int P\,dV$?
options: Quasistatic processes need no heat exchange, so $W=\Delta U$ holds and the integral is unnecessary.
The gas must stay near equilibrium so that a single pressure $P(V)$ exists throughout the integral.
Slow processes are always isothermal, which is what makes the integral easy to evaluate.
The work depends on how fast the piston moves, so we must pick the slowest possible speed.
p7-l003-first-law-quasistatic-work.explanation: For rapid compression the gas near the piston has a higher pressure than the bulk and the work done is larger than $-\int P\,dV$ calculated from the average pressure.

p7-l003-first-law-quasistatic-work.prompt: A piston compresses 1.00 mol of ideal gas isothermally and quasistatically at 300 K to half its initial volume. How much work is done on the gas? Give the answer in J.
p7-l003-first-law-quasistatic-work.explanation: $W=-\int P\,dV=nRT\ln(V_i/V_f)=nRT\ln2\approx1.73$ kJ, positive because the surroundings do work on the gas; the same amount leaves as heat so $\Delta U=0$.

p7-l003-first-law-quasistatic-work.prompt: Explain why the work done on a gas between two states depends on the path taken while the change in internal energy does not. Use a PV diagram in your answer.
p7-l003-first-law-quasistatic-work.rubric: Full credit requires: $U$ is a state function fixed by the end states; $W=-\int P\,dV$ is the area under the path on a PV diagram, which differs between paths; so $Q=\Delta U-W$ also differs between paths.
p7-l003-first-law-quasistatic-work.modelAnswer: $U$ depends only on the state, so $\Delta U$ is the same for every path. The work is minus the area under the $P(V)$ curve, which depends on the route taken. Since $Q=\Delta U-W$, the heat is path dependent as well.

p7-l004-adiabatic-compression.prompt: A bicycle pump gets hot when you inflate a tire quickly. Which explanation is correct?
options: Friction between the piston and the cylinder walls alone is responsible for the heating.
Heat flows into the gas from the warmer surrounding air during the compression.
The pressure itself is a source of heat, so any increase in pressure raises the temperature.
The compression is nearly adiabatic: work raises the internal energy before heat can escape.
p7-l004-adiabatic-compression.explanation: With $Q\approx0$, $\Delta U=W>0$, so $T$ rises. This is the principle of diesel ignition and of cooling by sudden expansion.

p7-l004-adiabatic-compression.prompt: In a diesel engine, air at 300 K is compressed adiabatically and quasi-statically by a factor of 15 in volume. For a diatomic gas, $\gamma=1.4$. Using $TV^{\gamma-1}=$ const, what is the final temperature? Give it in K.
p7-l004-adiabatic-compression.explanation: $T_f=300\times15^{0.4}=886$ K, hot enough to ignite the injected fuel without a spark.

p7-l004-adiabatic-compression.prompt: Starting from the first law and the equipartition result $U=\tfrac f2NkT$, explain how to arrive at $PV^\gamma=$ const for a quasistatic adiabatic process of an ideal gas.
p7-l004-adiabatic-compression.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) adiabatic means Q=0 so dU = -P dV; (2) dU = (f/2)Nk dT and PV = NkT give (f/2) dT/T = -dV/V; (3) integrating yields T V^(2/f) = const, i.e. T V^(gamma-1) with gamma = (f+2)/f, hence P V^gamma = const.
p7-l004-adiabatic-compression.modelAnswer: With $Q=0$: $dU=-P\,dV$. Using $dU=\tfrac f2Nk\,dT$ and $P=NkT/V$: $\tfrac f2\,dT/T=-dV/V$. Integrating gives $TV^{2/f}=$ const, and since $\gamma=(f+2)/f$ we have $2/f=\gamma-1$, so $TV^{\gamma-1}=$ const; using $T\propto PV$ gives $PV^\gamma=$ const.

p7-l005-heat-capacities-calorimetry.prompt: For an ideal gas, why is $C_P$ larger than $C_V$ by $Nk$?
options: At constant $P$ the gas expands and does work, so extra heat is needed beyond the rise in $U$.
Because pressure itself stores energy, a gas held at constant pressure has more energy to raise.
Because gases at constant pressure have extra degrees of freedom that are absent at constant volume.
Because $C_V$ includes the work done by the gas, while $C_P$ counts only the change in internal energy.
p7-l005-heat-capacities-calorimetry.explanation: $C_P=C_V+Nk$: part of the heat goes into $P\,dV$ work. For solids and liquids the expansion is tiny so $C_P\approx C_V$.

p7-l005-heat-capacities-calorimetry.prompt: A 50.0 g copper block at 100.0 $^\circ$C is dropped into 100.0 g of water at 20.0 $^\circ$C in an insulated cup. Ignoring the cup, what is the final temperature? Use $c_{Cu}=385$ J/(kg K) and $c_{w}=4186$ J/(kg K). Give it in $^\circ$C.
p7-l005-heat-capacities-calorimetry.explanation: Energy balance: $m_{Cu}c_{Cu}(100-T)=m_wc_w(T-20)$, giving $T\approx23.5\,^\circ$C. The small copper block barely warms the large heat capacity of the water.

p7-l005-heat-capacities-calorimetry.prompt: Explain why $C_P$ exceeds $C_V$ for a gas, yet the two are almost equal for a solid or a liquid.
p7-l005-heat-capacities-calorimetry.rubric: Full credit requires: at constant $P$ a gas expands and does work $P\,dV$ against the surroundings, so extra heat is needed; solids and liquids change volume very little on heating, so little work is done and $C_P\approx C_V$.
p7-l005-heat-capacities-calorimetry.modelAnswer: Heating at constant pressure lets a gas expand, so part of the heat goes into $P\,dV$ work and $C_P=C_V+Nk$. A solid or liquid expands only slightly on heating, so almost no work is done and $C_P\approx C_V$.

p7-l006-enthalpy-latent-heat.prompt: During boiling at atmospheric pressure, you keep adding heat to water at 100 $^\circ$C but the temperature doesn't change. Where does the energy go?
options: It is stored as kinetic energy of the water molecules, which then move faster than before.
It is lost to the surroundings, so the water stays at 100 $^\circ$C because it cools as fast as it heats, so no energy is left over to heat the water.
It goes into overcoming intermolecular attractions in the liquid-to-vapour change, not into kinetic energy.
The thermometer is faulty, because the heat capacity of water drops to zero at 100 $^\circ$C.
p7-l006-enthalpy-latent-heat.explanation: At a phase transition, heat changes the structure (the potential-energy part of $U$) at constant $T$; the heat capacity is formally infinite.

p7-l006-enthalpy-latent-heat.prompt: A chemist measures the heat released by a reaction in an open flask (constant atmospheric pressure). Which quantity does this measure?
options: The internal energy change $\Delta U$, whatever the conditions under which the reaction is run.
The Gibbs free energy change $\Delta G$, since the flask is open and the reaction is spontaneous.
The entropy change $\Delta S$, since the heat released is always divided by the temperature.
The enthalpy change $\Delta H$, since $Q_P=\Delta H$ at constant pressure.
p7-l006-enthalpy-latent-heat.explanation: $H=U+PV$ and $dH=T\,dS+V\,dP$, so at constant $P$ the heat absorbed equals $\Delta H$ (assuming only $PV$ work).

p7-l006-enthalpy-latent-heat.prompt: How much heat is needed to warm 0.50 kg of liquid water from 20 $^\circ$C to 100 $^\circ$C and then vaporize 0.10 kg of it? Use $c=4186$ J/(kg K) and $L_v=2.257\times10^{6}$ J/kg. Give the answer in kJ.
p7-l006-enthalpy-latent-heat.explanation: $Q=mc\Delta T+m'L_v=167.4+225.7=393.1$ kJ. Note the vaporisation of only 20% of the water needs more energy than heating all of it by 80 K.

p7-l006-enthalpy-latent-heat.prompt: Explain, in your own words, what enthalpy is and why chemists use it rather than internal energy.
p7-l006-enthalpy-latent-heat.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) H = U + PV; (2) at constant pressure the heat absorbed equals Delta H, because the PV work is accounted for; (3) most lab chemistry occurs at constant (atmospheric) pressure, so Delta H is what a calorimeter measures.
p7-l006-enthalpy-latent-heat.modelAnswer: Enthalpy is $H=U+PV$, the energy of the system plus the work needed to make room for it at pressure $P$. At constant pressure, $dH=dU+P\,dV=\delta Q$, so $\Delta H$ is exactly the heat exchanged. Because most chemistry happens at atmospheric pressure, $\Delta H$ (not $\Delta U$) is what a calorimeter measures.

p7-l007-microstates-two-state-counting.prompt: Flip four fair coins. Why is 'two heads, two tails' the most probable macrostate even though 'HHTT' is no more likely than 'HHHH' as a specific sequence?
options: Fair coins prefer to land in equal numbers, so an even split is the likeliest outcome.
Each sequence is equally likely, but 'two heads' contains 6 microstates and 'four heads' only 1.
Because the specific sequence HHTT is more likely than HHHH when the coins are fair.
Because the macrostate is chosen to maximise the energy of the coin system.
p7-l007-microstates-two-state-counting.explanation: Probability of a macrostate = (number of its microstates)/(total microstates). Entropy counts exactly this.

p7-l007-microstates-two-state-counting.prompt: What does the fundamental assumption of statistical mechanics say?
options: All macrostates are equally probable, whatever the number of microstates each contains.
The system always sits in its lowest-energy microstate, which is the most probable one.
In an isolated system in equilibrium, every accessible microstate is equally probable.
Microstates with higher energy are more probable, because there are more ways to reach them.
p7-l007-microstates-two-state-counting.explanation: Equal weights on microstates imply that macrostates with more microstates are more likely: the origin of the second law.

p7-l007-microstates-two-state-counting.prompt: Flip 10 fair coins. What is the probability of getting exactly 5 heads? Give it as a decimal between 0 and 1.
p7-l007-microstates-two-state-counting.explanation: There are $\binom{10}{5}=252$ microstates with 5 heads out of $2^{10}=1024$ equally likely sequences, so $P=252/1024\approx0.246$.

p7-l007-microstates-two-state-counting.prompt: For 100 fair coins, explain the difference between a microstate and a macrostate, and why a result near 50 heads is overwhelmingly more likely than 100 heads.
p7-l007-microstates-two-state-counting.rubric: Full credit requires: a microstate is the specific head/tail sequence, a macrostate is the number of heads; all microstates are equally likely; the macrostate with 50 heads contains vastly more microstates ($\sim10^{29}$) than the single microstate for 100 heads.
p7-l007-microstates-two-state-counting.modelAnswer: A microstate is the exact sequence of heads and tails; a macrostate only records how many heads there are. Every sequence is equally likely, but 50 heads corresponds to about $10^{29}$ sequences whereas 100 heads corresponds to exactly one, so near-even splits dominate.

p7-l008-einstein-solid-entropy.prompt: Two independent systems have multiplicities $\Omega_1$ and $\Omega_2$. Why is entropy $S=k\ln\Omega$ additive?
options: The combined multiplicity is the product $\Omega_1\Omega_2$, and the log turns it into a sum.
Because multiplicities add when independent systems are combined, so their logarithms add too.
Because the logarithm is only defined for sums, so entropy must be defined as a sum of terms.
It isn't additive: the entropy of the combined system equals the larger of the two entropies.
p7-l008-einstein-solid-entropy.explanation: The logarithm is exactly what makes entropy extensive. $k$ sets the units (J/K).

p7-l008-einstein-solid-entropy.prompt: An Einstein solid has $N=10$ oscillators sharing $q=10$ quanta. The multiplicity is $\Omega=\binom{q+N-1}{q}$. What is the entropy $S/k=\ln\Omega$? (Dimensionless.)

A sample contains $N$ nuclear spins-1/2 in a magnetic field. If all spin orientations are equally likely (no polarization), how many microstates are there, and what is the entropy? What happens to the entropy when the spins become partially aligned?
p7-l008-einstein-solid-entropy.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) 2^N microstates, S = k ln 2^N = N k ln 2; (2) alignment reduces the number of microstates (fewer arrangements with a given excess in the lower state); (3) entropy is lower for the polarised ensemble.
p7-l008-einstein-solid-entropy.modelAnswer: Each spin has two states, so there are $2^N$ microstates and $S=k\ln2^N=Nk\ln2$. Partial alignment concentrates the population into fewer microstates ($\Omega=\binom{N}{N_\uparrow}$ is smaller), so the entropy is lower. Polarising spins (as in NMR) costs entropy.

p7-l009-two-einstein-solids.prompt: Two Einstein solids exchange energy quanta. At equilibrium the most probable arrangement is the one where:
options: The energy per oscillator is nearly equal in both, so the larger solid holds proportionally more quanta.
All the energy sits in the smaller solid, because it can reach a given temperature with fewer quanta, and so can hold much more energy per quantum.
The two solids hold equal numbers of quanta, regardless of how many oscillators each contains.
All the energy sits in the larger solid, because it has far more ways to hold the quanta.
p7-l009-two-einstein-solids.explanation: The product $\Omega_A\Omega_B$ is maximised when the temperatures (slopes of $\ln\Omega$) match, i.e. when the energy per oscillator is equal.

p7-l009-two-einstein-solids.prompt: Solid A has 300 oscillators and solid B has 200. Together they hold 100 energy quanta. In the most probable state, how many quanta are in solid A?
p7-l009-two-einstein-solids.explanation: At equilibrium the energy per oscillator is equal: $q_A/N_A=q_B/N_B$, so $q_A=100\times300/500=60$.

p7-l009-two-einstein-solids.prompt: Two Einstein solids of different sizes exchange energy quanta. Explain why the most probable arrangement has equal energy per oscillator rather than equal energy in each solid.
p7-l009-two-einstein-solids.rubric: Full credit requires: total multiplicity is the product $\Omega_A\Omega_B$; it is maximised when shifting a quantum does not change $\ln\Omega_{total}$; this occurs when both solids have the same energy per oscillator, so the larger solid holds proportionally more.
p7-l009-two-einstein-solids.modelAnswer: The total multiplicity $\Omega_A\Omega_B$ is largest when the energy sharing makes the two solids equally 'eager' to take energy, which happens at equal energy per oscillator. The larger solid therefore holds proportionally more of the energy.

p7-l010-stirling-sharp-peaks-irreversibi.prompt: Why do macroscopic systems never spontaneously 'un-mix' or have heat flow from cold to hot, even though the microscopic dynamics permit it?
options: Because the laws of mechanics forbid such motions, so they never occur in any real system.
Because the second law is a fundamental force that pushes systems toward higher entropy.
Such states are not impossible but overwhelmingly improbable: the multiplicity peak is so sharp.
Because the molecules somehow know which direction time flows and arrange their motion to follow it.
p7-l010-stirling-sharp-peaks-irreversibi.explanation: The multiplicity curve for $N\sim10^{23}$ is so narrow that the probability of a macroscopic deviation is like $e^{-10^{20}}$.

p7-l010-stirling-sharp-peaks-irreversibi.prompt: The relative width of the multiplicity peak scales as $1/\sqrt N$. Estimate the relative width for $N=10^{23}$ particles (give the number).
p7-l010-stirling-sharp-peaks-irreversibi.explanation: $1/\sqrt{10^{23}}=3.16e-12$: fluctuations are about $3\times10^{-12}$ of the mean, undetectable.

p7-l010-stirling-sharp-peaks-irreversibi.prompt: Why does Stirling's approximation help show that the multiplicity function is sharply peaked? Explain how you get from $\Omega$ to a Gaussian.
p7-l010-stirling-sharp-peaks-irreversibi.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) factorials in binomial-type multiplicity are approximated by N! ~ N^N e^-N sqrt(2 pi N); (2) ln Omega near its maximum is expanded to second order, giving Omega ~ Omega_max exp(-(x-x0)^2 / 2 sigma^2); (3) sigma/mean scales as 1/sqrt N, so the peak is extremely sharp for large N.
p7-l010-stirling-sharp-peaks-irreversibi.modelAnswer: Stirling, $\ln N!\approx N\ln N-N$, turns factorial multiplicities into smooth functions. Expanding $\ln\Omega$ to second order about its maximum gives $\Omega\approx\Omega_{max}\exp[-(x-x_0)^2/2\sigma^2]$, a Gaussian. Because $\ln\Omega$ is extensive, the width relative to the mean scales as $1/\sqrt N$, so for macroscopic $N$ the peak is extremely narrow.

p7-l011-counting-states-sackur-tetrode.prompt: Why does the Sackur-Tetrode derivation divide the count of states by $N!$?
options: To correct for the collisions between particles, which would otherwise be counted twice.
Identical particles are indistinguishable, so swapping labels gives no new microstate.
Because each molecule has $N$ translational degrees of freedom, all of which must be divided out.
To account for the fact that the total energy of the isolated gas is conserved.
p7-l011-counting-states-sackur-tetrode.explanation: Dividing by $N!$ makes $S$ proportional to $N$ at fixed density, as it must be.

p7-l011-counting-states-sackur-tetrode.prompt: An ideal gas of $N$ particles is allowed to occupy twice the volume at fixed $N$ and fixed energy. By what factor does its multiplicity $\Omega$ change?
options: $2$, since doubling the volume doubles the number of available states.
$2^N$, since every particle independently has twice as many positions.
$2N$, since each of the $N$ particles gains one extra region.
$2^{3N/2}$, since volume enters like the kinetic energy of the gas.
p7-l011-counting-states-sackur-tetrode.explanation: Each of the $N$ particles has a position-space factor $V$, so $\Omega\propto V^N$ and doubling $V$ multiplies $\Omega$ by $2^N$ (the energy dependence is a separate factor).

p7-l011-counting-states-sackur-tetrode.prompt: Using $S=Nk[\ln(V/N\lambda^3)+\tfrac52]$, so that heating at constant volume gives $\Delta S=\tfrac32 Nk\ln(T_2/T_1)$, find the entropy change of 1.00 mol of monatomic ideal gas heated at constant volume from 300 K to 600 K. Give it in J/K.
p7-l011-counting-states-sackur-tetrode.explanation: Entropy depends on temperature through $\tfrac32Nk\ln T$: $\Delta S=\tfrac32R\ln2\approx8.64$ J/K.

p7-l011-counting-states-sackur-tetrode.prompt: Outline the logic that leads from counting the states of one particle in a box to the Sackur-Tetrode entropy of $N$ particles, including where the factor $1/N!$ enters.
p7-l011-counting-states-sackur-tetrode.rubric: Full credit requires: single-particle states counted by position volume times momentum-space volume over $h^3$; $N$ particles give $V^N$ times a $3N$-dimensional momentum sphere at fixed energy; divide by $N!$ for indistinguishable particles; then $S=k\ln\Omega$ with Stirling's approximation.
p7-l011-counting-states-sackur-tetrode.modelAnswer: One particle in a box has states labelled by position and momentum, counted as phase-space volume over $h^3$. For $N$ particles the positions give $V^N$ and the momenta give the volume of a $3N$-dimensional sphere at fixed energy. Dividing by $N!$ removes the overcounting of identical particles, and $S=k\ln\Omega$ with Stirling's formula gives Sackur-Tetrode.

p7-l012-expansion-mixing-absolute-entrop.prompt: A gas expands freely (no work, no heat) into twice its volume. What is the entropy change?
options: $\Delta S=0$, since no heat flows into the gas during the process.
$\Delta S<0$, because the gas spreads out and becomes more ordered after the expansion.
$\Delta S=Nk\ln2$ only if the gas does work on its surroundings as it expands.
$\Delta S=Nk\ln2>0$: each molecule gets twice the space, although $Q=0$.
p7-l012-expansion-mixing-absolute-entrop.explanation: Free expansion is irreversible. Because $S$ is a state function, we can compute $\Delta S$ along any reversible path between the same states: $\int P\,dV/T=Nk\ln(V_2/V_1)$.

p7-l012-expansion-mixing-absolute-entrop.prompt: Two identical samples of the same gas, at the same $T$ and $P$, are separated by a partition. After removing the partition, what is the entropy change?
options: $2Nk\ln2$, exactly as for the mixing of two different gases at the same temperature and pressure.
$Nk\ln2$, since the molecules from one side can now explore the other half of the volume.
Zero: the final state is just a larger sample at the same density.
Negative, since removing the partition lets the gas organise itself uniformly in the larger volume.
p7-l012-expansion-mixing-absolute-entrop.explanation: For different gases each species expands into twice the volume, giving $2Nk\ln 2$. For identical gases nothing macroscopic changes: this is the resolution of the Gibbs paradox.

p7-l012-expansion-mixing-absolute-entrop.prompt: Use the Sackur-Tetrode equation $S=Nk[\ln(V/N\lambda^3)+\tfrac52]$ with $\lambda=h/\sqrt{2\pi mkT}$ to compute the molar entropy of argon ($m=39.948$ u) at 298.15 K and 1 bar. Give the answer in J/(mol K).
p7-l012-expansion-mixing-absolute-entrop.explanation: $\lambda=16.00$ pm, $V/N=kT/P$; the result $154.8$ J/(mol K) agrees with the tabulated 154.8.

p7-l012-expansion-mixing-absolute-entrop.prompt: In your own words, what is the Gibbs paradox and how does counting identical particles resolve it?
p7-l012-expansion-mixing-absolute-entrop.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) without a 1/N! factor, mixing two samples of the same gas would produce an entropy increase of 2Nk ln 2, even though nothing observable has changed; (2) identical molecules are indistinguishable, so permutations don't yield distinct microstates, giving a 1/N! factor; (3) this makes entropy extensive and removes the spurious mixing entropy.
p7-l012-expansion-mixing-absolute-entrop.modelAnswer: If you treat molecules as distinguishable, removing a partition between two samples of the *same* gas appears to raise the entropy by $2Nk\ln2$, although nothing has changed physically and the process is reversible. The fix is that identical molecules are indistinguishable: permuting them gives the same microstate, so we divide by $N!$. Then $S$ is extensive and mixing identical gases gives zero entropy change.

p7-l013-second-law-entropy-changes.prompt: Which is the best statement of the statistical second law?
options: Isolated systems tend toward macrostates with the most microstates; entropy decreases are astronomically improbable.
The entropy of an isolated system can never fluctuate downward, even for a system of just 10 particles.
The entropy of any system, isolated or not, always increases with time without exception.
Heat can never flow from cold to hot under any circumstances, including inside a refrigerator.
p7-l013-second-law-entropy-changes.explanation: The law is statistical: for few particles fluctuations are visible, but for $N\sim10^{23}$ they are unobservable.

p7-l013-second-law-entropy-changes.prompt: A hot block at $T_h$ is placed in contact with a cold block at $T_c$ and heat $Q$ flows from hot to cold. What happens to the total entropy?
options: It is unchanged, since energy is conserved when heat moves from one block to the other.
It decreases, because the hot block loses entropy and heat flow orders the system.
It increases only if the two blocks are made of different materials with different heat capacities.
It increases: the cold block gains $Q/T_c$, more than the hot block's loss $Q/T_h$.

p7-l013-second-law-entropy-changes.prompt: 1.00 kg of water is heated reversibly from 20 $^\circ$C (293.15 K) to 80 $^\circ$C (353.15 K). With $c=4186$ J/(kg K) constant, what is its entropy change $\Delta S=C\ln(T_2/T_1)$? Give it in J/K.
p7-l013-second-law-entropy-changes.explanation: $\Delta S=4186\ln(353.15/293.15)=779$ J/K. (Using the average temperature, $Q/T_{avg}=251\,160/323=777$ J/K, is close but not exact.)

p7-l013-second-law-entropy-changes.prompt: Heat flowing from a cold body to a hot body would conserve energy, yet it is never observed. Explain why, using microstates or entropy.
p7-l013-second-law-entropy-changes.rubric: Full credit requires: the total entropy would decrease ($-Q/T_c+Q/T_h<0$); equivalently the final macrostate has far fewer microstates than the initial one, so it is overwhelmingly improbable; energy conservation alone does not select the direction.
p7-l013-second-law-entropy-changes.modelAnswer: Moving $Q$ from cold to hot changes the entropy by $Q/T_h-Q/T_c<0$, so the combined system would end in a macrostate with far fewer microstates. Such a transition is not forbidden by energy conservation but is overwhelmingly improbable, which is what the second law states.

p7-l014-entropy-information-arrow-of-tim.prompt: Microscopic laws are time-reversal invariant, yet we observe an arrow of time. What is the resolution?
options: Microscopic laws are not really time-reversal invariant, and that asymmetry gives the arrow of time.
The universe began in a very low-entropy state, and high-entropy microstates vastly outnumber the rest.
Reversed motions are physically impossible, as they would violate the equations of motion themselves, since a reversed film of the motion could not occur in nature.
Time is only defined for macroscopic systems, so a microscopic law has no direction to be reversed.
p7-l014-entropy-information-arrow-of-tim.explanation: Reversed trajectories exist but occupy an exceedingly small fraction of phase space; the arrow comes from boundary conditions plus counting.

p7-l014-entropy-information-arrow-of-tim.prompt: A system has $\Omega$ equally likely microstates. How is the information you are missing about its exact microstate, in bits, related to its entropy?
options: The missing information is $\log_2\Omega$ bits, and $S=(k\ln2)\times$ (bits).
The missing information is $\Omega$ bits, and $S$ grows in proportion to $\Omega$.
The missing information is $\ln\Omega$ bits, and $S=$ (bits)$/kT$.
The missing information is $N$ bits, independent of $\Omega$, as only the particle count matters.
p7-l014-entropy-information-arrow-of-tim.explanation: Specifying one of $\Omega$ equally likely microstates takes $\log_2\Omega$ bits, and $S=k\ln\Omega=(k\ln2)\log_2\Omega$, so entropy is missing information in units of $k\ln2$ per bit.

p7-l014-entropy-information-arrow-of-tim.prompt: Explain how entropy is related to information, and why knowing more about a system's microstate reduces the entropy you assign to it.
p7-l014-entropy-information-arrow-of-tim.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) entropy S = k ln Omega measures the number of microstates consistent with what we know about the macrostate, i.e. missing information; (2) if we learn more about the microstate (fewer possibilities), Omega falls and so does the entropy we assign; (3) mention of bits (k ln 2 per bit) or Maxwell's demon.
p7-l014-entropy-information-arrow-of-tim.modelAnswer: $S=k\ln\Omega$ measures how many microstates are compatible with the macrostate we know, i.e. how much information about the microstate is missing (each bit corresponds to $k\ln2$). If we acquire information that narrows the possible microstates, $\Omega$ and the assigned entropy decrease, which is why Maxwell's demon must pay an entropy cost to acquire and erase information.

p7-l015-temperature-as-ds-du.prompt: Why does equating the slopes $\partial S/\partial U$ of two systems in thermal contact give the equilibrium condition?
options: Because entropy is conserved in the exchange, so the total entropy stays the same throughout.
Total multiplicity is maximal when shifting a little energy leaves $S_{total}$ unchanged: equal slopes, equal $T$.
Because energy flows until the entropies of the two systems are equal to each other.
Because energy flows until the internal energies of the two systems are equal to each other.
p7-l015-temperature-as-ds-du.explanation: Energy flows to the system with the larger $\partial S/\partial U$ (the colder one), since it gains more entropy than the other loses. Hence $1/T=\partial S/\partial U$.

p7-l015-temperature-as-ds-du.prompt: The Einstein solid's $T(U)$ rises with $U$ (positive heat capacity). What does this say about the shape of $S(U)$?
options: $S(U)$ is concave: each added unit of energy raises $S$ by less than the one before.
$S(U)$ is convex, so each added unit of energy raises the entropy more than the one before.
$S(U)$ is a straight line, with a slope that is the same at every energy.
$S$ decreases with $U$ at all energies, which is why the temperature increases.
p7-l015-temperature-as-ds-du.explanation: $T^{-1}=\partial S/\partial U$ decreasing with $U$ means $\partial^2S/\partial U^2<0$: concavity, which guarantees stable thermal equilibrium.

p7-l015-temperature-as-ds-du.prompt: For a monatomic ideal gas $S=\tfrac32Nk\ln U+\text{const}$ at fixed $V$ and $N$. For $N=1.00$ mol with $U=3.74$ kJ, find $T$ from $1/T=\partial S/\partial U$. Give it in K.
p7-l015-temperature-as-ds-du.explanation: $\partial S/\partial U=\tfrac{3Nk}{2U}=1/T$ gives $U=\tfrac32NkT$, so $T=2U/(3Nk)\approx300$ K, recovering equipartition.

p7-l015-temperature-as-ds-du.prompt: Derive, in words and symbols, why the quantity $\partial S/\partial U$ plays the role of inverse temperature when two systems exchange energy.
p7-l015-temperature-as-ds-du.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) total entropy S1(U1)+S2(U2) with U1+U2 fixed; (2) maximise: dS = (1/T1 - 1/T2) dU1 = 0 gives equal slopes; (3) the slope is therefore the quantity that is equalised, and energy flows from the smaller slope (hot) to the larger slope (cold), consistent with 1/T = dS/dU.
p7-l015-temperature-as-ds-du.modelAnswer: With $U_1+U_2$ fixed, the total entropy $S_1(U_1)+S_2(U_2)$ is maximal when $\partial S_1/\partial U_1=\partial S_2/\partial U_2$. Energy flows toward the system for which an energy gain raises $S$ more (larger slope). The quantity that equalises at equilibrium and decides the direction of energy flow is what we call inverse temperature: $1/T=\partial S/\partial U$.

p7-l016-negative-temperature-entropy-fro.prompt: A spin system with population inversion (more spins in the upper level than in the lower) has a negative absolute temperature. What does this mean when it is placed in contact with an ordinary system?
options: It is colder than absolute zero and absorbs energy from any ordinary system it touches.
Nothing happens, because negative temperatures cannot be defined for any physical system at all.
It would violate energy conservation, so such a state cannot be prepared in a real experiment.
It is hotter than any positive temperature: energy flows from it into an ordinary system.
p7-l016-negative-temperature-entropy-fro.explanation: Negative $T$ arises because adding energy to a bounded spectrum can decrease $S$ ($\partial S/\partial U<0$). On the scale of $\beta=1/kT$ it lies beyond $+\infty$.

p7-l016-negative-temperature-entropy-fro.prompt: Below 10 K the heat capacity of an insulating crystal follows $C=bT^3$ with $b=2.0\times10^{-4}$ J/K$^4$. Using $S(T)=\int_0^TC/T'\,dT'$ with $S(0)=0$, find $S$ at $T=10$ K. Give it in J/K.
Explain how a measured heat capacity $C(T)$ lets you determine the absolute entropy of a substance, and what role the third-law convention $S(0)=0$ plays.
p7-l016-negative-temperature-entropy-fro.rubric: Full credit requires: $dS=C\,dT/T$ for reversible heating, so $S(T)=\int_0^TC/T'\,dT'$ plus the entropy at $T=0$; the third law fixes that constant to zero for a perfect crystal; this gives absolute entropies from calorimetry.
p7-l016-negative-temperature-entropy-fro.modelAnswer: Reversible heating gives $dS=C\,dT/T$, so integrating measured $C(T)/T$ from near $0$ up to $T$ gives the entropy. The third law sets $S(0)=0$ for a perfect crystal, which fixes the integration constant and yields absolute entropies.

p7-l017-two-state-paramagnet-curie-law.prompt: Why does the magnetisation of a paramagnet follow the Curie law $M\propto B/T$ at high temperature?
options: Because heating generates additional magnetic moments in the sample, which add to the magnetisation.
Because the dipoles are completely aligned at high $T$, so the magnetisation reaches its maximum.
Thermal agitation randomises the dipoles, so only a fraction $\sim\mu B/kT$ is aligned.
Because the field strength itself depends on temperature, falling as the sample is warmed up.
p7-l017-two-state-paramagnet-curie-law.explanation: For $\mu B\ll kT$, $\tanh(\mu B/kT)\approx\mu B/kT$. The competition is energy ($\mu B$) versus entropy ($kT$).

p7-l017-two-state-paramagnet-curie-law.prompt: Electron spins ($\mu=9.274\times10^{-24}$ J/T) sit in a 1.00 T field at 300 K. For a two-state paramagnet, what is the magnetisation as a fraction of saturation, $M/N\mu=\tanh(\mu B/kT)$? Give the dimensionless value.
p7-l017-two-state-paramagnet-curie-law.explanation: $\mu B/kT\approx2.24\times10^{-3}\ll1$, so $\tanh x\approx x$: only about 0.22% of saturation, the Curie regime.

p7-l017-two-state-paramagnet-curie-law.prompt: Explain, in terms of the competition between energy and entropy, why a paramagnet shows Curie behaviour ($M\propto B/T$) at high temperature but saturates at low temperature.
p7-l017-two-state-paramagnet-curie-law.rubric: Full credit requires: aligned dipoles lower the energy; disorder maximises entropy; at high $T$ thermal energy $kT\gg\mu B$ keeps nearly random orientations so only a small fraction $\sim\mu B/kT$ is aligned; at low $T$ energy wins and all dipoles align (saturation).
p7-l017-two-state-paramagnet-curie-law.modelAnswer: Alignment with the field lowers the energy by $\mu B$ per spin, but disorder raises the entropy. At high $T$ the thermal energy $kT$ far exceeds $\mu B$, so only a fraction $\sim\mu B/kT$ is aligned (Curie). At low $T$ the energy term wins and all spins align, giving saturation.

p7-l018-nmr-polarization-negative-temper.prompt: Why do NMR spectroscopists want ever-stronger magnets (and sometimes cooled probes)?
options: The molecules need stronger fields to be excited into the upper spin state at all.
Stronger fields raise the temperature of the sample, which increases the population difference.
Stronger fields make Boltzmann statistics irrelevant, so all spins then contribute to the signal.
The signal follows the excess in the lower spin state, which grows as $B/T$.
p7-l018-nmr-polarization-negative-temper.explanation: Polarisation $\approx\hbar\gamma B/2kT$ is only about $10^{-5}$ at room temperature, so every increase helps.

p7-l018-nmr-polarization-negative-temper.prompt: A spin-1/2 system in a field has more nuclei in the *upper* energy state than the lower. Which statement is correct?
options: It is colder than absolute zero, and therefore cannot exist as an equilibrium state of any system.
It has a negative temperature, can release energy (as a laser does), and is hotter than any positive $T$.
It is at infinite entropy, since all the spins are equally likely to be in either state.
It is impossible to prepare, since population inversion violates the second law of thermodynamics.
p7-l018-nmr-polarization-negative-temper.explanation: Population inversion is routine in NMR (after a 180 degree pulse) and lasing; the temperature is formally negative since $n_\uparrow/n_\downarrow=e^{-\Delta E/kT}>1$.

p7-l018-nmr-polarization-negative-temper.prompt: Protons in a 11.74 T magnet precess at 500 MHz, so the spin-state energy gap is $\Delta E=h\nu$. At 298.15 K, what is the fractional polarisation $P=\tanh(\Delta E/2kT)$ (difference of populations divided by their sum), in parts per million?
p7-l018-nmr-polarization-negative-temper.explanation: $\Delta E=3.31\times10^{-25}$ J, $\Delta E/2kT=4.0\times10^{-5}$, so $P\approx40.2$ ppm: only 40 of every million spins contribute net signal.

p7-l018-nmr-polarization-negative-temper.prompt: Explain why NMR is intrinsically an insensitive technique, using the Boltzmann population of the two spin states.
p7-l018-nmr-polarization-negative-temper.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the energy gap between spin states is tiny compared with kT at room temperature (about 10^-5), so populations are nearly equal; (2) only the small population excess (about B/T times a constant) produces a net signal; (3) so signal grows with B and falls with T.
p7-l018-nmr-polarization-negative-temper.modelAnswer: The two nuclear-spin levels are separated by an energy $\Delta E=\hbar\gamma B$ that is about $10^{-5}kT$ at room temperature, so the Boltzmann populations are almost equal. Only the tiny excess $\Delta E/2kT\sim10^{-5}$ in the lower state gives a net signal, and it scales as $B/T$, which is why strong magnets and low temperatures help.

p7-l019-pressure-from-entropy.prompt: Two gases are separated by a movable, heat-conducting piston. What determines the equilibrium position of the piston?
options: The two sides have equal volumes, since the piston moves until it is exactly in the middle.
The two sides hold equal numbers of molecules, whatever their temperatures or volumes.
Total entropy is maximal: $P_1/T_1=P_2/T_2$, which for equal $T$ means equal $P$.
The side with the larger entropy always wins, so the piston moves to enlarge that side.
p7-l019-pressure-from-entropy.explanation: The thermodynamic definition: $P/T=(\partial S/\partial V)_{U,N}$. Volume flows to the side where it gains more entropy.

p7-l019-pressure-from-entropy.prompt: From the ideal-gas entropy $S=Nk\ln V+\cdots$ at fixed $U$ and $N$, which relation follows?
options: $P/T=\partial S/\partial V=Nk/V$, i.e. $PV=NkT$.
$P=0$, because the entropy depends only on the logarithm of the volume and not on the energy.
$PV=U$, since the entropy's volume dependence fixes the energy in terms of the pressure.
$P=T\ln V$, since the entropy is proportional to $\ln V$ and $P/T=S/V$.
p7-l019-pressure-from-entropy.explanation: The ideal-gas law is purely a statement that the multiplicity of positions grows as $V^N$.

p7-l019-pressure-from-entropy.prompt: Derive the relation $P/T=(\partial S/\partial V)_{U,N}$ from the condition for mechanical equilibrium of two systems that can exchange volume (and energy).
p7-l019-pressure-from-entropy.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) total S = S1(U1,V1) + S2(U2,V2) with V1+V2 and U1+U2 fixed; (2) at maximum, dS = (1/T1 - 1/T2) dU1 + (P1/T1 - P2/T2) dV1 = 0; (3) so the volume derivative of entropy (dS/dV)_U = P/T is what equalises; with T equal this means equal pressure.
p7-l019-pressure-from-entropy.modelAnswer: With $V_1+V_2$ and $U_1+U_2$ fixed, maximising $S_1+S_2$ over $V_1$ and $U_1$ gives $\left(\partial S_1/\partial V_1\right)_U=\left(\partial S_2/\partial V_2\right)_U$ and $\partial S_1/\partial U_1=\partial S_2/\partial U_2$. Identifying $(\partial S/\partial V)_U=P/T$ (which reproduces $PV=NkT$ for the ideal gas), the first condition becomes equal pressure when the temperatures are equal.

p7-l020-thermodynamic-identity-reversibl.prompt: The thermodynamic identity is $dU=T\,dS-P\,dV$. For a reversible process, which interpretation is correct?
options: $T\,dS$ is the heat added and $-P\,dV$ is the work done on the system.
$T\,dS$ is the work done and $-P\,dV$ is the heat added, since $P\,dV$ is a heat term.
Both terms are heat, since each is an energy change that comes from a thermal exchange.
Both terms are work, since each is the product of an intensive and an extensive quantity.
p7-l020-thermodynamic-identity-reversibl.explanation: For quasistatic processes, $\delta Q=T\,dS$ and $\delta W=-P\,dV$. For irreversible processes $\delta Q<T\,dS$.

p7-l020-thermodynamic-identity-reversibl.prompt: 1.00 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K expands isothermally and reversibly to twice its volume. Using $Q=T\Delta S$ with $\Delta S=nR\ln(V_2/V_1)$, how much heat does it absorb? Give it in J.
p7-l020-thermodynamic-identity-reversibl.explanation: $Q=nRT\ln2=1729$ J. Since $\Delta U=0$, all of it becomes work done by the gas.

p7-l020-thermodynamic-identity-reversibl.prompt: The identity $dU=T\,dS-P\,dV$ lets you read $T\,dS$ as heat. Explain why this identification holds only for reversible processes, using the free expansion of a gas as an example.
p7-l020-thermodynamic-identity-reversibl.rubric: Full credit requires: in free expansion $Q=0$ and $W=0$ but $\Delta S>0$, so $T\,dS\neq\delta Q$; $dU=T\,dS-P\,dV$ is a relation between state functions, valid along any reversible path between the same end states; $T\,dS=\delta Q$ only when the process is reversible.
p7-l020-thermodynamic-identity-reversibl.modelAnswer: In free expansion no heat flows, yet the entropy increases, so $T\,dS\ne\delta Q$. The identity relates state functions and holds for any pair of nearby equilibrium states, but identifying $T\,dS$ with heat and $-P\,dV$ with work requires a reversible path.

p7-l021-diffusive-equilibrium-definition.prompt: Two containers hold the same ideal gas at the same temperature but different concentrations, and are joined by a small hole. In which direction do particles tend to flow, and what quantity decides it?
options: From low to high concentration, in order to equalise the pressure on the two sides.
They don't flow at all, because the two containers are at the same temperature.
From the concentrated side to the dilute side, as $\mu=kT\ln(n/n_Q)$ is higher there.
From low to high $\mu$, because the particles move toward the state with more available entropy.
p7-l021-diffusive-equilibrium-definition.explanation: Particle flow raises total entropy when it goes from larger $-\partial S/\partial N$ to smaller. Equal $\mu$ means diffusive equilibrium.

p7-l021-diffusive-equilibrium-definition.prompt: In the identity $dU=T\,dS-P\,dV+\mu\,dN$, what does $\mu$ represent?
options: The energy needed to add one particle at fixed entropy and volume.
The entropy gained when one particle is added at fixed energy.
The heat absorbed when one particle is added at fixed temperature.
The pressure change caused by adding one particle at fixed volume.
p7-l021-diffusive-equilibrium-definition.explanation: Setting $dS=dV=0$ gives $\mu=(\partial U/\partial N)_{S,V}$, the energy cost of adding a particle without changing the entropy or volume.

p7-l021-diffusive-equilibrium-definition.prompt: Explain why the equality of chemical potentials is the condition for equilibrium between two phases or two regions that exchange particles.
p7-l021-diffusive-equilibrium-definition.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) mu = -T dS/dN measures the entropy cost/gain of moving a particle; (2) with total N fixed, S_total is maximised when mu1 = mu2; otherwise particles moving from higher to lower mu raise S_total; (3) so coexistence of phases (and chemical equilibrium) requires equal mu.
p7-l021-diffusive-equilibrium-definition.modelAnswer: $\mu=-T(\partial S/\partial N)$ tells how much entropy a region gains when it takes in a particle. With the total number fixed, particles flow until a further transfer cannot increase $S_{total}$, i.e. until $\mu_1=\mu_2$. For two phases in coexistence, and for reacting species ($\sum\nu_i\mu_i=0$), the same condition applies.

p7-l022-mu-of-ideal-gas-and-chemical-equ.prompt: If you compress an ideal gas isothermally to a higher pressure, what happens to its chemical potential?
options: It decreases, because compressing the gas reduces the volume available to each particle.
It increases by $kT\ln(P_2/P_1)$.
It stays the same, since $T$ is fixed and $\mu$ depends on temperature alone.
It becomes independent of $N$, since compression fixes the number of particles per unit volume.
p7-l022-mu-of-ideal-gas-and-chemical-equ.explanation: $\mu=\mu^\circ+kT\ln(P/P^\circ)$: higher pressure means a stronger 'escaping tendency' for particles.

p7-l022-mu-of-ideal-gas-and-chemical-equ.prompt: A chemist states that the molar Gibbs energy $G/n$ is the chemical potential. Is that consistent with the statistical-mechanics definition $\mu=-T(\partial S/\partial N)_{U,V}$?
options: No: $\mu$ is the molar enthalpy, and Gibbs energy is a different quantity altogether.
No: $\mu$ is the molar entropy, as the definition involves the derivative of $S$.
No: $\mu$ has nothing to do with Gibbs energy, which is defined only for chemical reactions.
Yes: $\mu=(\partial G/\partial N)_{T,P}$ is the partial molar Gibbs energy; the definitions agree.
p7-l022-mu-of-ideal-gas-and-chemical-equ.explanation: From $dU=TdS-PdV+\mu dN$ and Legendre transforms: $dG=-SdT+VdP+\mu dN$.

p7-l022-mu-of-ideal-gas-and-chemical-equ.prompt: A gas at 298.15 K is compressed isothermally from 1 bar to 10 bar. What is the change in chemical potential per mole, $\Delta\mu=RT\ln(P_2/P_1)$? Give it in kJ/mol.
p7-l022-mu-of-ideal-gas-and-chemical-equ.explanation: $\Delta\mu=RT\ln10=5.71$ kJ/mol. This is the Gibbs-energy cost of compressing each mole.

p7-l022-mu-of-ideal-gas-and-chemical-equ.prompt: Explain, in terms of entropy, why the chemical potential of an ideal gas rises with concentration at fixed temperature and falls with temperature at fixed concentration.
p7-l022-mu-of-ideal-gas-and-chemical-equ.rubric: Full credit requires: $\mu=kT\ln(n\lambda^3)$; more particles per volume means adding another particle gains less entropy, so $\mu$ (energy cost at fixed $S$, $V$) rises; at higher $T$ the thermal wavelength $\lambda$ shrinks and $\ln(n\lambda^3)$ becomes more negative, lowering $\mu$.
p7-l022-mu-of-ideal-gas-and-chemical-equ.modelAnswer: With $\mu=kT\ln(n\lambda^3)$, a denser gas has a larger $\mu$ because each added particle finds fewer new states, so it gains less entropy. At higher temperature the thermal wavelength $\lambda$ is smaller, so more states are available per particle and $\mu$ falls.

p7-l023-carnot-efficiency-second-law.prompt: Why can no heat engine operating between $T_h$ and $T_c$ be more efficient than a Carnot engine?
options: Because Carnot engines have no friction, so their parts waste nothing and real engines cannot match them.
Because the first law forbids any engine from converting heat into more work than the Carnot engine.
Such an engine would drive a Carnot refrigerator and move heat cold-to-hot with no net work.
Because Carnot engines use an ideal gas as their working substance, which no other fluid can beat.
p7-l023-carnot-efficiency-second-law.explanation: $e_{Carnot}=1-T_c/T_h$ is an upper bound for all engines between those temperatures: the proof is by contradiction with the second law.

p7-l023-carnot-efficiency-second-law.prompt: A real engine achieves a lower efficiency than the Carnot limit. Which is the underlying reason?
options: Irreversible processes (friction, finite temperature differences, rapid expansion) generate entropy.
The first law is violated in real engines, since some of the energy supplied is lost as heat.
Real engines have no cold reservoir, so they cannot reject any heat to the surroundings.
Efficiency can only be computed for ideal gases, so a real engine's value is simply not defined, whereas real working fluids have no efficiency at all.
p7-l023-carnot-efficiency-second-law.explanation: Carnot efficiency needs reversible heat transfer at nearly the same temperature, which means zero power output.

p7-l023-carnot-efficiency-second-law.prompt: Derive the Carnot efficiency from the second law, explaining the role of entropy.
p7-l023-carnot-efficiency-second-law.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) engine takes heat Qh from hot reservoir and rejects Qc to cold; W = Qh - Qc; (2) for a reversible cycle total entropy change is zero: Qh/Th = Qc/Tc; (3) thus e = W/Qh = 1 - Qc/Qh = 1 - Tc/Th, and irreversibility makes Qc larger, so e smaller.
p7-l023-carnot-efficiency-second-law.modelAnswer: The engine takes $Q_h$ from the hot reservoir and discards $Q_c$ to the cold one, so $W=Q_h-Q_c$. For a reversible cycle the total entropy change is zero: $-Q_h/T_h+Q_c/T_c=0$, giving $Q_c/Q_h=T_c/T_h$. Therefore $e=1-Q_c/Q_h=1-T_c/T_h$. Any irreversibility generates entropy and forces larger $Q_c$, hence lower efficiency.

p7-l024-cycles-refrigerators.prompt: An Otto-cycle engine with compression ratio $r=9$ and working gas with $\gamma=1.4$ has efficiency $e=1-r^{1-\gamma}$. What is its efficiency? Give it as a percentage.
p7-l024-cycles-refrigerators.explanation: $e=1-9^{-0.4}=0.585$, i.e. 58.5% for the ideal cycle. Real engines reach about 30%.

p7-l024-cycles-refrigerators.prompt: A refrigerator keeps its interior at 268 K in a kitchen at 298 K. What is the maximum possible coefficient of performance $T_c/(T_h-T_c)$ (heat removed per unit work)?
p7-l024-cycles-refrigerators.explanation: $COP_{max}=268/30=8.93$. Cooling to a smaller temperature difference is much more efficient.

p7-l024-cycles-refrigerators.prompt: Why does the coefficient of performance of a refrigerator get worse as the kitchen gets hotter, with its interior held at the same temperature?
options: The Carnot limit $T_c/(T_h-T_c)$ falls as the temperature gap grows.
The refrigerant carries less heat per cycle whenever the room is warm.
The compressor loses efficiency because hot air is less dense.
The interior leaks heat faster, which reduces work in the cycle.
p7-l024-cycles-refrigerators.explanation: The best possible COP is $T_c/(T_h-T_c)$, so a larger lift between the inside and the kitchen means more work per unit of heat removed.

p7-l024-cycles-refrigerators.prompt: Explain why the net work of an engine cycle equals the area enclosed on a PV diagram, and why some heat must always be rejected to the cold reservoir.
p7-l024-cycles-refrigerators.rubric: Full credit requires: over a closed cycle $\Delta U=0$ so $W_{by}=Q_h-Q_c$; the work done by the gas over expansion minus compression is the enclosed area; the second law (entropy must not decrease, $Q_c/T_c\ge Q_h/T_h$) forbids $Q_c=0$.
p7-l024-cycles-refrigerators.modelAnswer: In a full cycle $\Delta U=0$, so net work out is $Q_h-Q_c$, and net $\int P\,dV$ is the enclosed area. Taking heat $Q_h$ from the hot reservoir lowers its entropy, so entropy must be dumped as $Q_c>0$ at $T_c$; otherwise total entropy would fall.

p7-l025-thermodynamic-potentials-legendr.prompt: A chemical reaction is carried out at constant temperature and pressure. Which potential is minimised at equilibrium?
options: The internal energy $U$, which is lowest in the ground state of the system.
The enthalpy $H=U+PV$, which would be minimal at fixed pressure and entropy.
The Helmholtz free energy $F=U-TS$, which is minimised at fixed volume.
The Gibbs free energy $G=U-TS+PV$, which is minimised at fixed $T$ and $P$.
p7-l025-thermodynamic-potentials-legendr.explanation: At fixed $T$ and $P$, the system plus its reservoir maximise total entropy exactly when $G$ of the system is minimised. For fixed $T$ and $V$ the analogue is $F$.

p7-l025-thermodynamic-potentials-legendr.prompt: The Haber reaction N$_2$ + 3H$_2\to$ 2NH$_3$ has $\Delta H^\circ=-92.2$ kJ/mol and $\Delta S^\circ=-198.8$ J/(mol K) at 298.15 K. Compute $\Delta G^\circ=\Delta H^\circ-T\Delta S^\circ$ in kJ/mol.
p7-l025-thermodynamic-potentials-legendr.explanation: $-T\Delta S=+59.3$ kJ/mol opposes the favourable $\Delta H=-92.2$ kJ/mol, giving $-32.9$ kJ/mol; at higher $T$ the entropy term would dominate and favour the reactants.

p7-l025-thermodynamic-potentials-legendr.prompt: Starting from the thermodynamic identity $dU=T\,dS-P\,dV$, explain how the Helmholtz free energy is obtained as a Legendre transform and what $dF$ is.
p7-l025-thermodynamic-potentials-legendr.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) F = U - TS replaces S by T as the natural variable; (2) dF = dU - T dS - S dT = -S dT - P dV; (3) hence F is minimal at constant T,V and (dF/dT)_V = -S, (dF/dV)_T = -P.
p7-l025-thermodynamic-potentials-legendr.modelAnswer: Define $F=U-TS$. Then $dF=dU-T\,dS-S\,dT=-S\,dT-P\,dV$, so $F$ is naturally a function of $(T,V)$. Its derivatives give $S=-(\partial F/\partial T)_V$ and $P=-(\partial F/\partial V)_T$. At constant $T$ and $V$ the system settles at the minimum of $F$.

p7-l026-maxwell-relations-free-energy-me.prompt: 'Free energy is the force toward equilibrium.' What is the physical meaning of this statement?
options: It means $G$ is a mechanical force that acts on the atoms and pushes them towards the products.
At fixed $T,P$, $\Delta S_{tot}=-\Delta G/T$, so a process is spontaneous exactly when it lowers $G$.
It means that the energy of the system is always minimised, whatever the conditions of the process, since a system always settles into its lowest-energy state.
It means that the entropy of the system alone is always minimised at equilibrium.
p7-l026-maxwell-relations-free-energy-me.explanation: The energy given to the reservoir ($-\Delta H$) changes the reservoir's entropy by $-\Delta H/T$; combined with the system's $\Delta S$ this gives $\Delta S_{tot}=-\Delta G/T$.

p7-l026-maxwell-relations-free-energy-me.prompt: The Maxwell relation $(\partial S/\partial V)_T=(\partial P/\partial T)_V$ is useful because:
options: It proves that entropy is a function of the volume alone, so it can be read off from $V$.
It turns an entropy derivative, which cannot be measured directly, into a measurable $\partial P/\partial T$.
It shows that the pressure of any substance is independent of its temperature at fixed volume.
It follows from the second law, but has no practical use for calculating real quantities.
p7-l026-maxwell-relations-free-energy-me.explanation: Maxwell relations follow from the equality of mixed partial derivatives of a potential (here $F$) and convert hard-to-measure derivatives into measurable ones.

p7-l026-maxwell-relations-free-energy-me.prompt: Explain the statement that free energy is the maximum work available from a system. Contrast Helmholtz free energy (constant $T,V$) with Gibbs free energy (constant $T,P$).
p7-l026-maxwell-relations-free-energy-me.rubric: Full credit requires: some energy must leave as heat $T\Delta S$ so only $\Delta F$ (or $\Delta G$) is available as work; $-\Delta F$ bounds total work at constant $T$; $-\Delta G$ bounds non-$PV$ work at constant $T,P$ (e.g. electrical work from a battery).
p7-l026-maxwell-relations-free-energy-me.modelAnswer: A system at fixed $T$ cannot convert all of $\Delta U$ to work because entropy changes force heat $T\Delta S$ to flow. The maximum work is $-\Delta F$ at constant $T,V$, and the maximum non-$PV$ work is $-\Delta G$ at constant $T,P$, as in electrochemical cells.

p7-l027-phase-diagrams-clausius-clapeyro.prompt: How is a pressure-temperature phase diagram of a pure substance related to the Gibbs free energy?
options: Phase diagrams are constructed from the enthalpy alone, with no reference to the entropy.
The stable phase at each $(T,P)$ is the one with the highest $G$ per molecule.
At phase boundaries the entropies of the two phases are equal, which is why they coexist.
At each $(T,P)$ the stable phase has the lowest $\mu=G/N$; boundaries are where two $\mu$ are equal.
p7-l027-phase-diagrams-clausius-clapeyro.explanation: Equal $\mu$ on both sides gives the coexistence curve $P(T)$ whose slope is the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.

p7-l027-phase-diagrams-clausius-clapeyro.prompt: Water boils at 100 $^\circ$C (373.15 K) at 1.013 bar. Using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation for an ideal vapour, $\ln(P_2/P_1)=-\frac{L}{R}\left(\frac1{T_2}-\frac1{T_1}\right)$ with $L=40.66$ kJ/mol, find the boiling temperature at 0.795 bar (a mountain town about 2000 m high). Give it in $^\circ$C.
p7-l027-phase-diagrams-clausius-clapeyro.explanation: $1/T_2=1/373.15-R\ln(0.795/1.013)/L$, giving $T_2=366.4$ K $=93.2$ $^\circ$C. Cooking takes longer at altitude.

p7-l027-phase-diagrams-clausius-clapeyro.prompt: Using the condition that the Gibbs free energies per molecule of two coexisting phases are equal along the boundary, explain how the Clausius-Clapeyron equation $dP/dT=L/(T\Delta V)$ arises.
p7-l027-phase-diagrams-clausius-clapeyro.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) along the boundary mu1(T,P) = mu2(T,P), so dmu1 = dmu2 as one moves along the boundary; (2) dmu = -s dT + v dP (per molecule), giving (s2 - s1) dT = (v2 - v1) dP; (3) with latent heat L = T(s2 - s1) one obtains dP/dT = L/(T Delta v).
p7-l027-phase-diagrams-clausius-clapeyro.modelAnswer: On the coexistence curve $\mu_1=\mu_2$, so $d\mu_1=d\mu_2$ along it. Using $d\mu=-s\,dT+v\,dP$ per molecule: $-s_1dT+v_1dP=-s_2dT+v_2dP$, so $dP/dT=(s_2-s_1)/(v_2-v_1)$. With latent heat per molecule $L=T(s_2-s_1)$ this is $dP/dT=L/(T\Delta v)$.

p7-l028-chemical-equilibrium-from-mu.prompt: For a reaction with $\Delta G^\circ=-10$ kJ/mol, a student says the reaction 'goes to completion'. What is the correct statement?
options: $K=e^{-\Delta G^\circ/RT}\approx57$: products favoured, some reactant remains, and $\Delta G=0$ at equilibrium.
Yes: a negative $\Delta G^\circ$ means that every reactant molecule is eventually converted.
No: $K<1$ for a negative $\Delta G^\circ$, so the reaction actually favours the reactants at equilibrium.
The reaction is at equilibrium initially, so the sign of $\Delta G^\circ$ has no effect on the composition, since the standard state is the equilibrium state in each case.
p7-l028-chemical-equilibrium-from-mu.explanation: $\Delta G=\Delta G^\circ+RT\ln Q=0$ at equilibrium. The sign of $\Delta G^\circ$ sets the *direction*, and its magnitude sets how extreme the ratio is.

p7-l028-chemical-equilibrium-from-mu.prompt: What equilibrium constant corresponds to $\Delta G^\circ=-10.0$ kJ/mol at 298.15 K? Use $K=\exp(-\Delta G^\circ/RT)$.
p7-l028-chemical-equilibrium-from-mu.explanation: $-\Delta G^\circ/RT=4.034$, so $K=56.5$. A change of just 5.7 kJ/mol shifts $K$ by a factor of 10.

p7-l028-chemical-equilibrium-from-mu.prompt: For the gas-phase reaction $2\mathrm{NO_2}\rightleftharpoons \mathrm{N_2O_4}$ at equilibrium, which relation between chemical potentials holds?
options: $\mu_{NO_2}=\mu_{N_2O_4}$, as each species equilibrates with the other.
$\mu_{N_2O_4}=2\mu_{NO_2}$, from $\sum_i\nu_i\mu_i=0$ for the reaction.
$\mu_{NO_2}=2\mu_{N_2O_4}$, as two NO$_2$ molecules disappear per dimer formed.
$\mu_{N_2O_4}=0$, because the product has reached its equilibrium amount.
p7-l028-chemical-equilibrium-from-mu.explanation: A reaction is at equilibrium when the Gibbs energy is stationary against extent of reaction: $\mu_{N_2O_4}-2\mu_{NO_2}=0$, weighting each chemical potential by its stoichiometric coefficient.

p7-l028-chemical-equilibrium-from-mu.prompt: Explain how the condition $\sum_i\nu_i\mu_i=0$ leads to an equilibrium constant $K=e^{-\Delta G^\circ/RT}$, and what that exponential dependence says about small changes in $\Delta G^\circ$.
p7-l028-chemical-equilibrium-from-mu.rubric: Full credit requires: $\mu_i=\mu_i^\circ+RT\ln a_i$ (ideal gas); inserting into $\sum\nu_i\mu_i=0$ gives $\ln K=-\Delta G^\circ/RT$; a change of $RT\approx2.5$ kJ/mol in $\Delta G^\circ$ changes $K$ by a factor $e$.
p7-l028-chemical-equilibrium-from-mu.modelAnswer: Writing $\mu_i=\mu_i^\circ+RT\ln a_i$ and imposing $\sum\nu_i\mu_i=0$ gives $\Delta G^\circ+RT\ln Q=0$, so at equilibrium $K=e^{-\Delta G^\circ/RT}$. Because of the exponential, each $RT\approx2.5$ kJ/mol shifts $K$ by a factor of $e$, so modest free-energy differences set large concentration ratios.

p7-l029-deriving-boltzmann-factor.prompt: Why is the probability of a small system being in state $s$ proportional to $e^{-E_s/kT}$ when it is in thermal contact with a large reservoir?
options: Because high-energy states are physically forbidden when a small system is in contact with a reservoir.
Because the small system always seeks the lowest energy available and so avoids high-energy states.
Energy $E_s$ taken from the reservoir cuts its microstates by a factor $e^{-E_s/kT}$.
Because probabilities must sum to one, which fixes the exponential form of the weights.

p7-l029-deriving-boltzmann-factor.prompt: What does the partition function $Z=\sum_se^{-E_s/kT}$ roughly measure?
options: The average energy of the system, since $Z$ weights each state by its energy.
It counts the effective number of thermally accessible states: $Z\to1$ at low $T$, large at high $T$.
The entropy of the system, since $Z$ measures the disorder directly in units of $k$.
The probability that the system is in its ground state, as the Boltzmann factor is normalised.
p7-l029-deriving-boltzmann-factor.explanation: $Z$ is the normalisation of the Boltzmann weights, and everything else in thermodynamics follows from it.

p7-l029-deriving-boltzmann-factor.prompt: Describe how the Boltzmann factor follows from the entropy of the reservoir, in your own words.
p7-l029-deriving-boltzmann-factor.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) system plus reservoir share a fixed total energy U; if the system takes energy E_s the reservoir has U - E_s; (2) the probability of that state is proportional to the number of reservoir microstates, exp[S_R(U - E_s)/k]; (3) expanding S_R to first order, dS_R/dU = 1/T gives exp(-E_s/kT).
p7-l029-deriving-boltzmann-factor.modelAnswer: If the small system is in state $s$ with energy $E_s$, the reservoir has energy $U-E_s$ and $\Omega_R(U-E_s)$ microstates. The probability is proportional to this. Writing $\Omega_R=e^{S_R/k}$ and expanding $S_R(U-E_s)\approx S_R(U)-E_s/T$ gives $P(s)\propto e^{-E_s/kT}$.

p7-l030-populations-from-boltzmann-facto.prompt: The first excited electronic state of a hydrogen atom lies 10.2 eV above the ground state. At room temperature ($kT\approx0.026$ eV), what is its thermal population?
options: About one percent, since the thermal energy is not far below the excitation energy, since $kT$ at room temperature is not far below the 10.2 eV gap.
About half, because the degeneracy of the excited state is four times larger.
About ten percent, because the excitation energy is only a few times $kT$.
Utterly negligible (of order $e^{-390}$): essentially every atom is in the ground state.
p7-l030-populations-from-boltzmann-facto.explanation: Even multiplying by a degeneracy factor of 4 cannot compensate for $e^{-10.2/0.026}$. Visible emission from H requires discharges or stars at thousands of kelvin.

p7-l030-populations-from-boltzmann-facto.prompt: The Cl$_2$ stretching vibration has wavenumber 560 cm$^{-1}$. At 300 K, what is the ratio of the population of the $v=1$ level to that of $v=0$, $e^{-hc\tilde\nu/kT}$? Use $hc/k=1.4388$ cm K.
p7-l030-populations-from-boltzmann-facto.explanation: $hc\tilde\nu/kT=1.4388\times560/300=2.686$, so the ratio is 0.0682: about 6.4% of Cl$_2$ molecules are vibrationally excited (hot bands in the spectrum).

p7-l030-populations-from-boltzmann-facto.prompt: A level sits $2kT$ above the ground state and is triply degenerate; the ground state is non-degenerate. What is the ratio of the total population of that level to that of the ground state?
options: About $0.41$
About $0.14$
About $0.045$
About $1.0$
p7-l030-populations-from-boltzmann-facto.explanation: Each of the three states has relative weight $e^{-2}=0.135$, so the level's total weight is $3e^{-2}\approx0.41$ times the ground state's. Degeneracy multiplies the Boltzmann factor.

p7-l030-populations-from-boltzmann-facto.prompt: A molecule has a ground state and an excited level at energy $\epsilon$. Explain what sets their population ratio, and what happens to the ratio as $T\to0$ and as $T\to\infty$.
p7-l030-populations-from-boltzmann-facto.rubric: Full credit requires: ratio $=g_2/g_1\,e^{-\epsilon/kT}$; as $T\to0$ all molecules are in the ground state; as $T\to\infty$ populations approach the ratio of degeneracies (equal if non-degenerate); the comparison is between $\epsilon$ and $kT$.
p7-l030-populations-from-boltzmann-facto.modelAnswer: The ratio is $e^{-\epsilon/kT}$ times the degeneracy ratio, so it depends on $\epsilon/kT$. At $T\to0$ everything sits in the ground state; as $T\to\infty$ the exponential tends to 1 and the populations approach the ratio of degeneracies.

p7-l031-mean-energy-from-z.prompt: How does the average energy of a system follow from its partition function?
options: $\langle E\rangle=kT\ln Z$, since the logarithm of $Z$ measures the energy per unit temperature.
$\langle E\rangle=Z/\beta$, since $Z$ divided by $\beta$ gives the typical energy of the system.
$\langle E\rangle=-\partial\ln Z/\partial\beta$, the Boltzmann-weighted mean of the energy.
$\langle E\rangle$ equals the smallest energy in the sum, because the ground state dominates.
p7-l031-mean-energy-from-z.explanation: Differentiating $Z=\sum e^{-\beta E_s}$ brings down $-E_s$ from each term, so $-\partial_\beta\ln Z=\sum E_se^{-\beta E_s}/Z$.

p7-l031-mean-energy-from-z.prompt: The mean energy of a quantum harmonic oscillator of frequency $\omega$ approaches what in the limits of high and low temperature?
options: $kT$ at high $T$; zero-point $\tfrac12\hbar\omega$ at low $T$ when $kT\ll\hbar\omega$.
$kT$ at both limits, since equipartition applies at every temperature to a harmonic oscillator.
Zero at low $T$ and $\hbar\omega$ at high $T$, since quantum effects switch on as the oscillator warms.
$\tfrac12kT$ at high $T$ and $kT$ at low $T$, with the roles of the two terms reversed.

p7-l031-mean-energy-from-z.prompt: A vibrational mode with wavenumber 1000 cm$^{-1}$ has heat capacity (Einstein function) $C/k=x^2e^x/(e^x-1)^2$ with $x=hc\tilde\nu/kT$. What is $C/k$ at 300 K? Use $hc/k=1.4388$ cm K.
p7-l031-mean-energy-from-z.explanation: $x=4.796$ so $C/k=0.193$, i.e. the mode contributes only 19% of its classical value $k$ at room temperature.

p7-l031-mean-energy-from-z.prompt: Explain why the mean energy of a system in thermal contact with a reservoir is $-\partial\ln Z/\partial\beta$, and what this tells you about why $Z$ is so useful.
p7-l031-mean-energy-from-z.rubric: Full credit requires: $\bar E=\sum E_se^{-\beta E_s}/Z$; the derivative $-\partial\ln Z/\partial\beta$ reproduces exactly this Boltzmann-weighted sum; $\ln Z$ therefore generates averages by differentiation, so one function carries the thermodynamics.
p7-l031-mean-energy-from-z.modelAnswer: The Boltzmann-weighted mean is $\sum E_se^{-\beta E_s}/Z$. Differentiating $\ln Z=\ln\sum e^{-\beta E_s}$ with respect to $\beta$ gives exactly $-\bar E$. So knowing $Z(\beta)$ yields averages by differentiation, which is why it is the central object.

p7-l032-equipartition-schottky-heat-capa.prompt: A two-level system (gap $\Delta$) has a heat capacity that peaks at a temperature of order $\Delta/2k$ and vanishes at both low and high $T$. Why does it vanish at high $T$?
options: At high $T$ both levels are equally populated, so the energy saturates and cannot absorb more.
Because the gap between the two levels closes at high temperature, so the system stops responding.
Because the system loses its energy to the surroundings faster than it can absorb heat.
Because the partition function diverges at high temperature, so the heat capacity is undefined.
p7-l032-equipartition-schottky-heat-capa.explanation: The energy is bounded (maximum $\Delta/2$ per system), so $C=dU/dT\to0$ when saturation is reached: the Schottky anomaly.

p7-l032-equipartition-schottky-heat-capa.prompt: Which term in a molecule's classical energy contributes an average of $\tfrac12kT$ according to the equipartition theorem?
options: The kinetic term $p_x^2/2m$ for one translational coordinate.
The gravitational term $mgz$, as every energy term gets $\tfrac12kT$.
A constant binding energy $-D$, as it is part of the molecule's energy.
A hard-wall confinement term, as it limits the available volume.
p7-l032-equipartition-schottky-heat-capa.explanation: Equipartition applies to terms quadratic in a coordinate or momentum. A linear term such as $mgz$ averages to $kT$, and a constant contributes no fluctuating energy at all.

p7-l032-equipartition-schottky-heat-capa.prompt: Show, for a degree of freedom whose energy is quadratic ($E=\alpha x^2$) and classical, that its average thermal energy is $\tfrac12kT$.
p7-l032-equipartition-schottky-heat-capa.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) Z = integral exp(-beta alpha x^2) dx proportional to beta^(-1/2) (Gaussian integral); (2) <E> = -d ln Z / d beta = 1/(2 beta) = kT/2; (3) independent of alpha: any quadratic term, which is the equipartition theorem; mention it requires classical continuous energies (kT >> level spacing).
p7-l032-equipartition-schottky-heat-capa.modelAnswer: $Z=\int e^{-\beta\alpha x^2}dx=\sqrt{\pi/\beta\alpha}\propto\beta^{-1/2}$. Then $\langle E\rangle=-\partial\ln Z/\partial\beta=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac1\beta=\tfrac12kT$, independent of $\alpha$. This holds only when the energy levels are dense compared with $kT$.

p7-l033-deriving-maxwell-distribution.prompt: If the temperature of a gas is raised, how does its Maxwell speed distribution change?
options: The distribution stays the same shape but is merely shifted to higher speeds.
The peak moves to lower speed, since the molecules lose energy to the walls.
The curve narrows and becomes taller, since the molecules become more alike in speed, since a hotter gas has molecules that are more alike in speed.
The peak moves up ($\propto\sqrt T$) and the curve broadens and lowers; the area stays 1.
p7-l033-deriving-maxwell-distribution.explanation: The factor $e^{-mv^2/2kT}$ cuts off at $v\sim\sqrt{kT/m}$ and the $v^2$ phase-space factor determines the shape.

p7-l033-deriving-maxwell-distribution.prompt: In the derivation of the Maxwell speed distribution, where does the factor $v^2$ come from?
options: The kinetic energy $\tfrac12mv^2$ appearing in the exponent of the Boltzmann factor.
The number of velocity vectors with speed $v$ grows with the area $4\pi v^2$ of a shell.
Collisions with the walls, whose rate grows with the square of the speed.
The normalisation constant, which must be fixed to make the area equal to one.
p7-l033-deriving-maxwell-distribution.explanation: Counting velocity vectors with speeds between $v$ and $v+dv$ uses a spherical shell of volume $4\pi v^2dv$. This growing factor multiplies the falling $e^{-mv^2/2kT}$.

p7-l033-deriving-maxwell-distribution.prompt: Why does the Maxwell speed distribution peak at a nonzero speed, and why does it fall off at high speed? Explain the two competing factors.
p7-l033-deriving-maxwell-distribution.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the number of velocity vectors with speed v grows as v^2 (spherical shell of volume 4 pi v^2 dv); (2) the Boltzmann factor exp(-mv^2/2kT) decreases with energy; (3) the product has a maximum at v = sqrt(2kT/m): few molecules are near zero speed (small shell) and few are at very high speed (Boltzmann suppression).
p7-l033-deriving-maxwell-distribution.modelAnswer: $f(v)\propto v^2e^{-mv^2/2kT}$. The $v^2$ comes from the phase space: the number of velocity vectors with speed in $[v,v+dv]$ is a shell of volume $4\pi v^2dv$. The exponential is the Boltzmann factor. At small $v$ the shell is small, at large $v$ the exponential kills the weight, so the product peaks at $v_{mp}=\sqrt{2kT/m}$.

p7-l034-characteristic-speeds-effusion-a.prompt: Hydrogen ($m=2$ u) and oxygen ($m=32$ u) escape through a tiny hole into vacuum at the same temperature. How do their effusion rates compare?
options: They effuse at the same rate, as the temperature is the same and the mean kinetic energy is shared.
Hydrogen effuses 16 times faster, since the rate scales as the inverse of the molecular mass.
Hydrogen effuses 4 times faster, as the rate goes as $1/\sqrt m$.
Oxygen effuses faster, because each oxygen molecule carries more energy than a hydrogen molecule.
p7-l034-characteristic-speeds-effusion-a.explanation: Graham's law: rate $\propto1/\sqrt m$, as the mean kinetic energies are equal.

p7-l034-characteristic-speeds-effusion-a.prompt: What is the correct order of the three characteristic speeds of the Maxwell distribution?
options: $v_{rms}<\bar v<v_{mp}$, since the rms is dominated by the slowest molecules.
$\bar v<v_{mp}<v_{rms}$, since the mean is pulled down by the slow molecules near zero speed.
All three are equal for a Gaussian-like distribution, as the peak coincides with the mean.
p7-l034-characteristic-speeds-effusion-a.explanation: The distribution has a long tail toward high speeds, which pulls the mean and rms above the peak.

p7-l034-characteristic-speeds-effusion-a.prompt: A reaction rate is proportional to the fraction of molecules with energy above the activation energy, $\propto e^{-E_a/RT}$. For $E_a=50$ kJ/mol, by what factor does the rate increase when the temperature rises from 298.15 K to 308.15 K?
p7-l034-characteristic-speeds-effusion-a.explanation: Ratio $=\exp[(E_a/R)(1/298.15-1/308.15)]=1.92$: the rule of thumb 'rates double per 10 K' is an average of this exponential sensitivity.

p7-l034-characteristic-speeds-effusion-a.prompt: Explain how the Maxwell distribution accounts for the Arrhenius form $e^{-E_a/RT}$ of reaction rates, and why the rate is so much more sensitive to temperature than the mean speed.
p7-l034-characteristic-speeds-effusion-a.rubric: Full credit requires: the rate is set by the fraction of molecules with energy above $E_a$ (the high-energy tail of the Boltzmann factor); the tail fraction $\sim e^{-E_a/kT}$ changes exponentially with $T$ while the mean speed changes only as $\sqrt T$.
p7-l034-characteristic-speeds-effusion-a.modelAnswer: Only molecules in the high-energy tail of the Boltzmann distribution, a fraction $\sim e^{-E_a/RT}$ per mole, can cross the barrier. That fraction changes exponentially with $T$, whereas the mean speed rises only as $\sqrt T$, which is why rates are so temperature sensitive.
