p7-l035-from-z-to-thermodynamics.prompt: Why is $Z_N=Z_1^N/N!$ for a gas of $N$ identical, non-interacting molecules but $Z_N=Z_1Z_2\cdots$ for $N$ distinguishable systems?
options: Because identical particles interact more strongly, which changes how their states are counted.
Because $N!$ is the number of molecules in a mole, so it only matters for macroscopic samples.
Identical gas particles are indistinguishable, so label permutations overcount microstates $N!$ times.
Because gas particles have fewer available states than the distinguishable systems found in solids, so they can be counted with a simpler formula, one that has no factorial.
p7-l035-from-z-to-thermodynamics.explanation: The $1/N!$ is what makes $F$ extensive and gives the Sackur-Tetrode entropy.

p7-l035-from-z-to-thermodynamics.prompt: Once you have $F=-kT\ln Z$, how do you obtain the pressure and entropy?
options: By integrating $F$ over $V$ and $T$, which gives the entropy and pressure directly.
They cannot be found from $F$ alone; one needs the energy distribution as well.
$S=F/T$ and $P=F/V$, since $F$ is the energy per unit temperature and volume.
As derivatives: $S=-(\partial F/\partial T)_{V,N}$ and $P=-(\partial F/\partial V)_{T,N}$.
p7-l035-from-z-to-thermodynamics.explanation: From $dF=-S\,dT-P\,dV+\mu\,dN$. The partition function therefore carries all the thermodynamics.

p7-l035-from-z-to-thermodynamics.prompt: Explain in your own words why all thermodynamic properties follow once you know the partition function $Z(T,V,N)$.
p7-l035-from-z-to-thermodynamics.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) Z encodes the Boltzmann-weighted sum over all microstates; (2) F = -kT ln Z is the thermodynamic potential for (T,V,N); (3) S, P, mu (and U, C_V) are partial derivatives of F, so one function gives everything.
p7-l035-from-z-to-thermodynamics.modelAnswer: $Z$ sums the Boltzmann weights of all microstates, so it contains the energy spectrum. $F=-kT\ln Z$ is the appropriate thermodynamic potential for fixed $(T,V,N)$, and from $dF=-S\,dT-P\,dV+\mu\,dN$, the entropy, pressure and chemical potential are its partial derivatives; $U$ and $C_V$ follow as well. Thus one function holds all the thermodynamics.

p7-l036-ideal-gas-and-diatomic-partition.prompt: For N$_2$ at 300 K, the rotational temperature is $\theta_{rot}\approx2.9$ K and the vibrational temperature is $\theta_{vib}\approx3400$ K. Which statement about its heat capacity is correct?
options: Translation and rotation are classical, so $C_V\approx\tfrac52Nk$; vibration is frozen out.
All three contribute fully, so $C_V=\tfrac72Nk$, since $T$ is larger than $\theta_{rot}$.
Only translation contributes, since rotation and vibration both need much higher temperatures.
Rotation is frozen, because $T\gg\theta_{rot}$ makes the rotational levels too closely spaced to matter.
p7-l036-ideal-gas-and-diatomic-partition.explanation: A mode is classical when $T\gg\theta$ and frozen when $T\ll\theta$.

p7-l036-ideal-gas-and-diatomic-partition.prompt: The classical rotational partition function of a homonuclear diatomic is $q_{rot}=T/(\sigma\theta_{rot})$ with symmetry number $\sigma=2$. For N$_2$ ($\theta_{rot}=2.88$ K) at 300 K, what is $q_{rot}$?
p7-l036-ideal-gas-and-diatomic-partition.explanation: $q_{rot}=300/(2\times2.88)=52.1$: about 52 rotational states are thermally accessible, which justifies the classical treatment.

p7-l036-ideal-gas-and-diatomic-partition.prompt: For the ideal gas $F=-kT\left[N\ln(V/N\lambda^3)+N\right]$. What does $P=-(\partial F/\partial V)_{T,N}$ give?
options: $P=NkT/V$, the ideal gas law.
$P=kT/V$, independent of the particle number.
$P=3NkT/2V$, from the kinetic energy of the gas.
$P=NkT/V^2$, from the volume dependence of the logarithm.
p7-l036-ideal-gas-and-diatomic-partition.explanation: Only the $-NkT\ln V$ term depends on $V$, so $P=NkT/V$. The ideal gas law follows from the partition function.

p7-l036-ideal-gas-and-diatomic-partition.prompt: For a diatomic gas, explain how the factorised partition function $Z_1=Z_{trans}Z_{rot}Z_{vib}$ explains why each kind of motion adds to the heat capacity only above its characteristic temperature.
p7-l036-ideal-gas-and-diatomic-partition.rubric: Full credit requires: $\ln Z$ is a sum so energies and heat capacities add; each factor behaves classically (contributing $\tfrac12kT$ per quadratic term) only when $T\gg$ its characteristic temperature ($\theta_{rot}\sim$ few K, $\theta_{vib}\sim10^3$ K); below that the mode is frozen into its ground state.
p7-l036-ideal-gas-and-diatomic-partition.modelAnswer: Because the factors multiply, $\ln Z$ and hence $U$ and $C_V$ add. Translation is classical at any realistic $T$; rotation turns on when $T\gg\theta_{rot}$ (a few K); vibration only when $T\gg\theta_{vib}$ (thousands of K). Below those temperatures the mode is stuck in its ground state.

p7-l037-gibbs-factor-fd-be-distributions.prompt: What is the maximum average occupation of a single-particle state for fermions and for bosons?
options: Both are limited to an occupation of at most 1, as a consequence of the Pauli principle.
Fermions: at most 1 (Pauli); bosons: unlimited, diverging as $\epsilon\to\mu$.
Fermions are unlimited and bosons are limited to at most 1, as bosons obey the exclusion rule.
Both are unlimited, since occupation is limited only by the available thermal energy.

p7-l037-gibbs-factor-fd-be-distributions.prompt: What does the Gibbs factor $e^{-(E-\mu N)/kT}$ add to the Boltzmann factor $e^{-E/kT}$?
options: It allows for the particle number of the small system to vary by exchange with the reservoir.
It accounts for the quantum indistinguishability of identical particles in the system.
It raises the effective temperature of the system above that of its surroundings.
It restricts each single-particle state to at most one occupying particle.
p7-l037-gibbs-factor-fd-be-distributions.explanation: Both energy and particles can flow to the reservoir; the reservoir's entropy cost for giving up energy $E$ and $N$ particles gives $e^{-(E-\mu N)/kT}$. Indistinguishability enters only through the allowed occupation numbers.

p7-l037-gibbs-factor-fd-be-distributions.prompt: Derive the Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein mean occupations from the Gibbs factor for a single state of energy $\epsilon$.
p7-l037-gibbs-factor-fd-be-distributions.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) Gibbs factor exp[-(E - mu N)/kT] for a state holding N particles of energy epsilon each; (2) fermions N = 0 or 1: nbar = x/(1+x) = 1/(e^{(eps-mu)/kT}+1) with x = e^{-(eps-mu)/kT}; (3) bosons N = 0, 1, 2, ...: geometric series gives nbar = 1/(e^{(eps-mu)/kT}-1).
p7-l037-gibbs-factor-fd-be-distributions.modelAnswer: With $x=e^{-(\epsilon-\mu)/kT}$, a state with $N$ particles has weight $x^N$. For fermions $N=0,1$: $Z=1+x$ and $\bar n=x/(1+x)=1/(x^{-1}+1)$. For bosons $N=0,1,2,\dots$: $Z=1/(1-x)$ and $\bar n=x/(1-x)=1/(x^{-1}-1)$.

p7-l038-classical-limit-spin-statistics.prompt: When can the quantum distributions be replaced by the classical Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution?
options: Whenever the particles are bosons, since bosons never feel the restrictions of the exclusion principle.
When every state has mean occupation far below 1: $n\lambda^3\ll1$ (dilute and hot).
Only at absolute zero, where all the particles sit in the lowest available states.
Whenever the particles are fermions, since their occupancy is already limited to a small number.

p7-l038-classical-limit-spin-statistics.prompt: How is the Pauli exclusion principle, as used in building electronic configurations, related to the Fermi-Dirac distribution?
options: It applies only to the nucleons inside nuclei and has no role in electronic structure.
It is an extra rule with no connection to statistics, added to explain the periodic table.
It means electrons repel each other so strongly that two can never share an orbital.
Electrons are spin-1/2 fermions, so an orbital holds one electron per spin state; FD is the thermal version.
p7-l038-classical-limit-spin-statistics.explanation: The spin-statistics theorem: half-integer spin implies antisymmetric wavefunctions, so no two identical fermions share a state.

p7-l038-classical-limit-spin-statistics.prompt: For N$_2$ gas at 300 K and 1 atm, the thermal de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda=h/\sqrt{2\pi mkT}$. Compute the degeneracy parameter $n\lambda^3$ (dimensionless) using $n=P/kT$ and $m=28.014$ u.
p7-l038-classical-limit-spin-statistics.explanation: $\lambda=19.0$ pm, $n=2.45\times10^{25}$ m$^{-3}$, so $n\lambda^3=1.7\times10^{-7}\ll1$: air is very classical.

p7-l038-classical-limit-spin-statistics.prompt: Explain why Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics describes N$_2$ gas at room temperature but fails for conduction electrons in a metal, using the degeneracy parameter $n\lambda^3$.
p7-l038-classical-limit-spin-statistics.rubric: Full credit requires: MB holds when mean occupation $\ll1$, i.e. $n\lambda^3\ll1$ (dilute or hot); for N$_2$ at 1 atm $n\lambda^3\sim10^{-7}$; for electrons in a metal the density is high and $m$ small so $\lambda$ is large, $n\lambda^3\gg1$ and Pauli exclusion matters.
p7-l038-classical-limit-spin-statistics.modelAnswer: MB is valid when states are rarely occupied, $n\lambda^3\ll1$. For N$_2$ at 1 atm this parameter is about $10^{-7}$. Conduction electrons have a high density and small mass (long $\lambda$), so $n\lambda^3\gg1$ and the Fermi-Dirac exclusion dominates.

p7-l039-density-of-states-fermi-energy.prompt: Copper has a conduction-electron density $n=8.49\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$. Compute its Fermi energy $E_F=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}(3\pi^2n)^{2/3}$ in eV. ($m_e=9.109\times10^{-31}$ kg)
p7-l039-density-of-states-fermi-energy.explanation: $E_F=7.04$ eV, corresponding to a Fermi temperature $T_F=E_F/k\approx81740$ K.

p7-l039-density-of-states-fermi-energy.prompt: In a free three-dimensional electron gas, how does the density of states $g(\epsilon)$ depend on energy?
options: It is constant in energy, as it is for a one-dimensional gas of electrons.
It grows as $\sqrt\epsilon$, because the states within radius $k$ scale as $k^3$.
It falls as $1/\sqrt\epsilon$, because high-energy states are harder to populate.
It grows linearly in $\epsilon$, because each state carries energy proportional to $\epsilon$.
p7-l039-density-of-states-fermi-energy.explanation: The number of $\mathbf k$-states inside a sphere of radius $k$ is $\propto k^3\propto\epsilon^{3/2}$, so $g=dN/d\epsilon\propto\sqrt\epsilon$.

p7-l039-density-of-states-fermi-energy.prompt: Explain how the Fermi energy arises when electrons fill states at $T=0$, and why $E_F\gg kT$ for the conduction electrons of a metal at room temperature.
p7-l039-density-of-states-fermi-energy.rubric: Full credit requires: the Pauli principle allows two electrons (spin up/down) per orbital state, so electrons fill the lowest states up to $E_F$ set by the electron density, $E_F\propto n^{2/3}$; in metals $E_F\sim$ several eV while $kT\approx0.026$ eV, so the electrons are strongly degenerate.
p7-l039-density-of-states-fermi-energy.modelAnswer: At $T=0$ electrons fill the lowest single-particle states, two per orbital, up to the Fermi energy fixed by the density, $E_F=(\hbar^2/2m)(3\pi^2n)^{2/3}$. In metals this is several eV, around 100 times $kT$ at room temperature, so the gas remains highly degenerate.

p7-l040-fermi-gas-heat-capacity-degenera.prompt: Why is the electronic heat capacity of a metal at room temperature much smaller than the classical value $\tfrac32Nk$?
options: Only electrons within about $kT$ of $E_F$ can be excited, a fraction $\sim1\%$; the rest are Pauli-blocked.
Electrons in metals carry no thermal energy, so they cannot contribute to the heat capacity.
Electrons have no kinetic energy at room temperature, so they cannot absorb thermal energy.
The electrons are frozen in place by the ion lattice, so they cannot take up thermal energy.
p7-l040-fermi-gas-heat-capacity-degenera.explanation: This is why $C_{el}\propto T$ and why classical equipartition fails for conduction electrons.

p7-l040-fermi-gas-heat-capacity-degenera.prompt: Why can white-dwarf stars support themselves against gravity even at low temperature?
options: Nuclear fusion continues in the core, which supplies the pressure that holds the star up.
The thermal pressure of the very hot gas, which stays high long after fusion has stopped.
Degenerate electrons are forced into high-momentum states by the Pauli principle, giving a pressure independent of $T$.
The electrons repel one another electrically with extreme strength when compressed.
p7-l040-fermi-gas-heat-capacity-degenera.explanation: Compression forces electrons into smaller $\Delta x$, raising their momenta. This sets the Chandrasekhar mass limit.

p7-l040-fermi-gas-heat-capacity-degenera.prompt: At 300 K the electronic heat capacity of a degenerate gas is $C=\frac{\pi^2}{2}Nk\,(kT/E_F)$. For copper ($E_F=7.04$ eV), what is $C/(Nk)$ at 300 K?
Sketch in words the density of states $g(\epsilon)\propto\sqrt\epsilon$ and the occupation $\bar n(\epsilon)$ at $T=0$ and at small $T>0$, and explain how this gives a heat capacity linear in $T$.
p7-l040-fermi-gas-heat-capacity-degenera.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) in 3D, g(epsilon) grows as the square root of epsilon (more states at higher energy); (2) at T=0 occupation is a step function up to E_F, at T>0 the step is smeared over about kT; (3) only about g(E_F) kT electrons are excited, each with energy ~kT, so U increases as T^2 and C = dU/dT is proportional to T.
p7-l040-fermi-gas-heat-capacity-degenera.modelAnswer: $g(\epsilon)\propto\sqrt\epsilon$ in three dimensions. At $T=0$ the occupation is a step: filled below $E_F$ and empty above. At small $T$ the step is smeared over a width $\sim kT$. The number of electrons affected is $\sim g(E_F)kT$, each gains $\sim kT$, so $\Delta U\propto T^2$ and $C=dU/dT\propto T$.

p7-l041-photon-gas-planck-distribution.prompt: Classical equipartition applied to the modes of radiation in a cavity predicts infinite total energy (the 'ultraviolet catastrophe'). How does quantisation fix this?
options: It reduces the number of modes to a finite number, by assumption rather than by a derivation.
It makes the speed of light depend on the temperature, which cuts off the high-frequency modes, which would then cut off the high-frequency modes as well.
It lowers the temperature of the cavity, so the equipartition result gives a finite energy.
Modes with $h\nu\gg kT$ cannot be excited, as energy comes in lumps $h\nu$; the spectrum is cut off.
p7-l041-photon-gas-planck-distribution.explanation: Each mode's average energy is $h\nu/(e^{h\nu/kT}-1)$, which tends to $kT$ at low frequency and to zero exponentially at high frequency.

p7-l041-photon-gas-planck-distribution.prompt: Why is the chemical potential of a photon gas in thermal equilibrium zero?
options: Photon number is not conserved, since the walls absorb and emit photons freely.
Photons are massless, so adding one costs no energy at any frequency.
Photons are bosons, and bosons always have a chemical potential of zero.
Photons do not interact, so the gas cannot exchange particles with a reservoir.
p7-l041-photon-gas-planck-distribution.explanation: Because the walls can create or destroy photons, equilibrium requires $\partial F/\partial N=\mu=0$. Photons being massless does not by itself fix $\mu$, which is what the number non-conservation does.

p7-l041-photon-gas-planck-distribution.prompt: Outline how the Planck spectrum follows from the density of cavity modes and the Bose-Einstein occupation, and show how it reduces to the classical Rayleigh-Jeans result at low frequency.
p7-l041-photon-gas-planck-distribution.rubric:
Full credit requires: mode density $\propto
u^2$ (two polarisations); each mode has mean energy $h
u/(e^{h
u/kT}-1)$; at low frequency this reduces to $kT$ (equipartition) giving $u\propto
u^2T$, and at high frequency the exponential suppresses the modes.
p7-l041-photon-gas-planck-distribution.modelAnswer:
Counting standing-wave modes gives a density $\propto
u^2$ with two polarisations. Each mode has mean energy $h
u/(e^{h
u/kT}-1)$ (BE with $\mu=0$). For $h
u\ll kT$ this is $kT$, giving Rayleigh-Jeans; for $h
u\gg kT$ the exponential cuts off the spectrum.

p7-l042-wien-stefan-boltzmann-applicatio.prompt: A tungsten lamp filament (about 2800 K) and the Sun (about 5800 K) are both approximately blackbodies. How do their spectra differ?
options: Both peak at the same wavelength, since a filament is a blackbody like the Sun.
The Sun peaks near 500 nm (visible); the filament near 1000 nm (infrared), so most lamp power is invisible.
The filament peaks at shorter wavelengths because it is brighter at close range.
The Sun peaks in the infrared, as the infrared is where the bulk of its energy is emitted.
p7-l042-wien-stefan-boltzmann-applicatio.explanation: Wien's law: $\lambda_{max}T=2.898$ mm K. Incandescent bulbs are inefficient for lighting.

p7-l042-wien-stefan-boltzmann-applicatio.prompt: If the temperature of a blackbody doubles, by what factor does the total radiated power per unit area change?
options: A factor of 2, because the power per unit area is proportional to the temperature.
A factor of 4, because the power per unit area is proportional to $T^2$.
A factor of 16, because the power per unit area goes as $T^4$.
A factor of 8, because the power per unit area is proportional to $T^3$.
p7-l042-wien-stefan-boltzmann-applicatio.explanation: Integrating the Planck spectrum gives $\sigma T^4$. The factor reflects both the peak moving up in frequency and more photons per mode.

p7-l042-wien-stefan-boltzmann-applicatio.prompt: Using Wien's law $\lambda_{max}T=2.898\times10^{-3}$ m K, find the peak wavelength emitted by a filament at 2800 K, in nm.
p7-l042-wien-stefan-boltzmann-applicatio.explanation: $\lambda_{max}=2.898\times10^{-3}/2800=1035$ nm (near infrared), well outside the visible range (400-700 nm).

p7-l042-wien-stefan-boltzmann-applicatio.prompt: Explain physically how the cosmic microwave background can be a blackbody spectrum at 2.7 K, and how Wien's law connects the temperature to the wavelength in the microwave band.
p7-l042-wien-stefan-boltzmann-applicatio.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the early universe was hot and in thermal equilibrium with radiation, giving a Planck spectrum; (2) expansion stretches wavelengths, lowering the effective temperature but preserving the blackbody shape; (3) Wien's law gives lambda_max = 2.898 mm K / 2.7 K, about 1 mm, i.e. microwaves.
p7-l042-wien-stefan-boltzmann-applicatio.modelAnswer: Early on, matter and radiation were in thermal equilibrium, so the radiation had a Planck spectrum. The universe's expansion redshifts all wavelengths by the same factor, which keeps a blackbody shape but with lower temperature, now 2.725 K. Wien's law gives $\lambda_{max}=2.898\text{ mm K}/2.725\text{ K}\approx1.06$ mm, in the microwave band.

p7-l043-debye-model-and-limits.prompt: At high temperature, what is the heat capacity of a solid in both models and why?
options: $3Nk$ (Dulong-Petit): six quadratic terms per atom, each contributing $\tfrac12kT$.
$\tfrac32Nk$, since only the three translational terms of each atom contribute classically.
$Nk$, since each atom has one effective oscillator contributing $kT$ to the energy.
It diverges, as every mode of the crystal becomes thermally accessible at high temperature.
p7-l043-debye-model-and-limits.explanation: At $T\gg\theta_D$ all modes are active and classical.

p7-l043-debye-model-and-limits.prompt: Using the Debye low-temperature law $C_V/Nk=\tfrac{12\pi^4}{5}(T/\theta_D)^3$, find $C_V/Nk$ at $T=10$ K for a solid with $\theta_D=400$ K. Give the dimensionless value.
p7-l043-debye-model-and-limits.explanation: $(T/\theta_D)^3=(1/40)^3=1.56\times10^{-5}$, and the prefactor $12\pi^4/5\approx234$ gives $C_V/Nk\approx3.7\times10^{-3}$, tiny compared with the Dulong-Petit value 3.

p7-l043-debye-model-and-limits.prompt: Explain, using the phonon picture, why the low-temperature heat capacity of an insulating solid goes as $T^3$.
p7-l043-debye-model-and-limits.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) at temperature T only phonons with energy hbar v q of order kT are thermally excited, so the excited modes fill a sphere in q-space of radius ~kT/hbar v; (2) the number of such modes is proportional to T^3, each carrying energy ~kT, so U is proportional to T^4; (3) C = dU/dT is proportional to T^3.
p7-l043-debye-model-and-limits.modelAnswer: Only phonons with $\hbar vq\lesssim kT$ are excited. In $q$-space they fill a sphere of radius $\propto T$, so their number scales as $T^3$, each carrying energy $\sim kT$. Hence $U\propto T^4$ and $C=dU/dT\propto T^3$.

p7-l044-einstein-vs-debye-debye-temperat.prompt: Why does the Einstein model of a solid fail at very low temperatures, while the Debye model succeeds?
options: The Einstein model has a single frequency, so $C$ falls exponentially; real solids have long-wave modes that stay excited ($T^3$).
The Einstein model neglects the quantisation of energy, and so cannot describe low temperatures.
Einstein's model predicts a $T^3$ law, which is too large compared with what is observed.
The Debye model neglects the atomic nature of solids, and so cannot be used at high temperature.
p7-l044-einstein-vs-debye-debye-temperat.explanation: Any $kT$, however small, can excite phonons whose energy $\hbar vq$ is smaller still: the density of low-energy states is what produces the power law.

p7-l044-einstein-vs-debye-debye-temperat.prompt: Diamond has a Debye temperature of about 2200 K, while lead's is about 100 K. What does this mean for their heat capacities at room temperature?
options: Both are at $3Nk$, since room temperature is high enough for every solid to follow Dulong-Petit.
Diamond is above $3Nk$, because its stiff bonds store more energy per atom than lead's.
Lead is at about $3Nk$, but diamond is far below because its stiff, high-frequency modes are frozen out.
Both are far below $3Nk$, since room temperature is below $\theta_D$ for each of the two solids.
p7-l044-einstein-vs-debye-debye-temperat.explanation: Light atoms and stiff bonds give high sound speeds and a high Debye temperature.

p7-l044-einstein-vs-debye-debye-temperat.prompt: Estimate the Debye temperature of diamond from $\theta_D=(\hbar v/k)(6\pi^2n)^{1/3}$, using an average sound speed of 13 000 m/s and an atomic density $n=1.76\times10^{29}$ m$^{-3}$. Give it in K.
p7-l044-einstein-vs-debye-debye-temperat.explanation: $(6\pi^2n)^{1/3}=2.19\times10^{10}$ m$^{-1}$ so $\theta_D\approx2169$ K, close to the tabulated 2230 K.

p7-l044-einstein-vs-debye-debye-temperat.prompt: Explain how a measured speed of sound lets you estimate the Debye temperature of a solid, and why stiff, light-atom solids such as diamond have a much higher $\theta_D$ than soft, heavy solids such as lead.
p7-l044-einstein-vs-debye-debye-temperat.rubric: Full credit requires: $\theta_D\propto v\,n^{1/3}$ (the cutoff frequency of the shortest allowed waves); stiff bonds and light atoms give a high sound speed; so diamond's modes have high frequencies and are frozen out at room temperature, while lead's are fully excited.
p7-l044-einstein-vs-debye-debye-temperat.modelAnswer: The cutoff phonon frequency is set by the sound speed and atomic density, $k\theta_D=\hbar v(6\pi^2n)^{1/3}$. Diamond's stiff bonds and light atoms give a large $v$, so $\theta_D\sim2000$ K and its modes are partly frozen at 300 K; lead's soft bonds give $\theta_D\sim100$ K, so it already follows Dulong-Petit.

p7-l045-bec-critical-temperature.prompt: Below the critical temperature of an ideal Bose gas, what happens to the number of particles in the ground state?
options: No particle is in the ground state, as the thermal energy spreads them over the excited states.
A macroscopic fraction piles into the lowest state, since the excited states hold only a limited number.
Only one particle occupies the ground state, the others being kept out by their mutual repulsion.
The ground state is empty, because bosons repel each other and avoid the state of lowest energy.
p7-l045-bec-critical-temperature.explanation: The excited states can accommodate at most $N_{ex}\propto T^{3/2}$ particles; the remainder must go to the ground state.

p7-l045-bec-critical-temperature.prompt: Estimate the BEC critical temperature of an ideal gas with the mass of $^4$He (4.0026 u) at the liquid density $n=2.18\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$, using $T_c=\frac{2\pi\hbar^2}{mk}\left(\frac{n}{2.612}\right)^{2/3}$. Give it in K.
p7-l045-bec-critical-temperature.explanation: $T_c\approx3.13$ K, remarkably close to the observed superfluid transition at 2.17 K, though helium is not an ideal gas.

p7-l045-bec-critical-temperature.prompt: Explain why an ideal Bose gas must put a macroscopic number of particles in the ground state below $T_c$. What limits the number that can sit in excited states?
p7-l045-bec-critical-temperature.rubric: Full credit requires: with $\mu\le0$ the excited states can hold at most $N_{exc}=V g_{3/2}(1)/\lambda^3\propto T^{3/2}$ particles; below $T_c$ this maximum is less than $N$, and the remainder must occupy the ground state.
p7-l045-bec-critical-temperature.modelAnswer: With $\mu\le0$ the excited states can hold at most $N_{exc}=(V/\lambda^3)g_{3/2}(1)$, which falls as $T^{3/2}$. Once this is less than $N$ the leftover particles have nowhere to go except the ground state, which then holds a macroscopic fraction.

p7-l046-condensate-wavefunction-bosons-v.prompt: At the same temperature and density, how do an ideal gas of fermions and an ideal gas of bosons differ near $T\to0$?
options: Both condense into the lowest state, since at $T\to0$ every particle seeks the lowest energy.
Both fill a Fermi sea, since the quantum statistics of the two kinds of gas are identical at $T=0$.
Fermions condense into the lowest state, whereas bosons spread out because they repel one another.
Fermions fill levels up to $E_F$ (a Fermi sea), whereas bosons pile into the lowest state.
p7-l046-condensate-wavefunction-bosons-v.explanation: Quantum statistics determines the ground state of non-interacting particles.

p7-l046-condensate-wavefunction-bosons-v.prompt: Which of these is a real example of Bose-Einstein condensation or the related superfluid transition?
options: Liquid water freezing at 0 $^\circ$C, a transition in which many molecules enter one ordered state.
Electrons in a copper wire at room temperature, which all move together as a single coherent state.
Ultracold rubidium atoms near 100 nK, and liquid $^4$He below 2.17 K.
Neutrinos in the early universe, which are bosons and therefore condensed into one quantum state.
p7-l046-condensate-wavefunction-bosons-v.explanation: Both involve bosonic atoms. Electrons are fermions and cannot condense in the same single-particle state (they pair up in superconductors).

p7-l046-condensate-wavefunction-bosons-v.prompt: What does it mean physically that a Bose-Einstein condensate can be described by a single macroscopic wavefunction?
p7-l046-condensate-wavefunction-bosons-v.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) a macroscopic number of particles occupy the same single-particle quantum state, so they share one wavefunction; (2) that gives phase coherence across the whole sample (interference, superfluid flow); (3) mention of a macroscopic quantum effect such as interference between two condensates or frictionless flow.
p7-l046-condensate-wavefunction-bosons-v.modelAnswer: Below $T_c$ a macroscopic fraction of the bosons sits in the same single-particle state, so they share a common wavefunction with a definite phase. The condensate is therefore coherent over the whole sample, which shows up as matter-wave interference between two condensates and as superfluid (frictionless) flow.

p7-l047-virial-expansion-van-der-waals.prompt: How does the second virial coefficient $B_2(T)$ of a real gas reflect the intermolecular potential?
options: It is negative at low $T$ (attraction dominates) and positive at high $T$ (repulsion dominates).
It is always zero, since the virial expansion for a gas contains only the ideal-gas term.
It is positive at low $T$, where the molecules are slow, and negative at high $T$.
It depends only on the molecular mass, not on the intermolecular potential or on the temperature.
p7-l047-virial-expansion-van-der-waals.explanation: $B_2=-\tfrac12\int(e^{-U/kT}-1)\,d^3r$. The Boyle temperature is where $B_2=0$: the gas behaves ideally to first order.

p7-l047-virial-expansion-van-der-waals.prompt: What physical effects do the parameters $a$ and $b$ in the van der Waals equation $(P+a n^2/V^2)(V-nb)=nRT$ represent?
options: $a$ is the volume of the molecules and $b$ is the strength of the attraction between them.
Both are corrections for the mass of the molecules, which makes real gases heavier than ideal ones.
$a$ and $b$ are both repulsive terms, which raise the pressure above the ideal-gas value.
$b$ is the excluded volume of the repulsive cores; $a$ is the attraction that lowers the pressure.
p7-l047-virial-expansion-van-der-waals.explanation: Hard cores shrink the free volume to $V-nb$; mean-field attractions reduce pressure by $a n^2/V^2$.

p7-l047-virial-expansion-van-der-waals.prompt: Explain how the van der Waals equation can be motivated from the second virial coefficient of a potential made of a hard core and a weak attractive tail.
p7-l047-virial-expansion-van-der-waals.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) B2 = b - a/(kT) for a hard core (excluded volume b) plus a weak attraction (integral gives a); (2) the virial expansion P/kT = n + B2 n^2 + ... ~ n(1 + n(b - a/kT)); (3) resumming gives P = nkT/(1 - nb) - a n^2, the van der Waals equation.
p7-l047-virial-expansion-van-der-waals.modelAnswer: A hard core of excluded volume $b$ and a weak long-range attraction give $B_2(T)\approx b-a/kT$. Then $P/kT=n+(b-a/kT)n^2+\dots$, which is the expansion of $P=nkT/(1-nb)-an^2$. Resumming the repulsive series into $1/(1-nb)$ gives the van der Waals equation.

p7-l048-vdw-critical-point-maxwell-const.prompt: Below the critical temperature, the van der Waals isotherm has a loop with a region of negative compressibility. What does the Maxwell equal-area construction do?
options: It removes the critical point, so that the isotherm is smooth at every temperature.
It replaces the loop by a horizontal line at the coexistence pressure, where $\mu_{liq}=\mu_{gas}$.
It picks the highest pressure reached on the loop, which marks the onset of liquefaction.
It averages the pressure over the loop with equal weight, giving the mean pressure of the isotherm.
p7-l048-vdw-critical-point-maxwell-const.explanation: The equal-area rule follows from $\mu_{liq}=\mu_{gas}$, since $\Delta\mu=\int V\,dP$ along the loop must vanish.

p7-l048-vdw-critical-point-maxwell-const.prompt: For the van der Waals gas the critical temperature is $T_c=8a/(27Rb)$. For CO$_2$, $a=0.364$ Pa m$^6$/mol$^2$ and $b=4.27\times10^{-5}$ m$^3$/mol. What is $T_c$ in K?
p7-l048-vdw-critical-point-maxwell-const.explanation: $T_c=303.8$ K, close to the measured 304.1 K, and shows how well simple physics (excluded volume plus weak attraction) captures real fluids.

p7-l048-vdw-critical-point-maxwell-const.prompt: Above the critical temperature, what do van der Waals isotherms in the $P$-$V$ plane look like?
options: They show a loop with a region of negative compressibility.
They fall monotonically with no loop and no distinct liquid and gas.
They contain a flat section at the coexistence pressure.
They rise with volume because repulsion dominates at high $T$.
p7-l048-vdw-critical-point-maxwell-const.explanation: Above $T_c$ the isotherms decrease monotonically, so $(\partial P/\partial V)_T<0$ everywhere and only one fluid phase exists; the loop appears only below $T_c$.

p7-l048-vdw-critical-point-maxwell-const.prompt: Explain why the Maxwell equal-area construction places the coexistence pressure where the two lobes of the van der Waals loop have equal area, using the equality of the chemical potentials of liquid and vapour.
p7-l048-vdw-critical-point-maxwell-const.rubric: Full credit requires: along an isotherm $d\mu=V\,dP/N$; liquid and vapour coexist when $\mu_{liq}=\mu_{vap}$, so $\oint V\,dP=0$ over the loop; this means the two lobes have equal area.
p7-l048-vdw-critical-point-maxwell-const.modelAnswer: At constant $T$, $d\mu=(V/N)\,dP$. Coexistence requires $\mu_{liq}=\mu_{vap}$, so the integral $\int V\,dP$ along the loop from liquid to vapour must vanish. That condition means the area between the isotherm and the horizontal line is equal above and below.

p7-l049-ising-model-transfer-matrix.prompt: What does the parameter $J>0$ in the Ising Hamiltonian $H=-J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j-h\sum_is_i$ represent?
options: The temperature of the lattice, which sets how strongly the neighbouring spins feel one another.
A coupling that favours parallel neighbours (ferromagnetic); $h$ is the external field.
The magnetisation of the lattice, which is the average of the spins taken over all the sites.
The cost of flipping one spin in zero field, regardless of what its neighbours are doing.
p7-l049-ising-model-transfer-matrix.explanation: The same model describes a lattice gas (occupied/empty sites with nearest-neighbour attraction) and cooperative binding (e.g. ligands on a polymer).

p7-l049-ising-model-transfer-matrix.prompt: In the 1D Ising chain at zero field the spin correlation falls as $\langle s_0s_r\rangle=\tanh^r(J/kT)$. For $J/kT=1.0$, what is the correlation length $\xi=-1/\ln\tanh(J/kT)$ in lattice spacings?
p7-l049-ising-model-transfer-matrix.explanation: $\tanh1=0.7616$, so $\xi=-1/\ln0.7616=3.67$ lattice spacings. As $T\to0$ ($J/kT\to\infty$) $\xi\to\infty$, a signature of order only at $T=0$.

p7-l049-ising-model-transfer-matrix.prompt: Explain why the transfer-matrix method turns the partition sum for a chain of $N$ coupled spins into a matrix power, and what the largest eigenvalue of the matrix determines.
p7-l049-ising-model-transfer-matrix.rubric: Full credit requires: the Boltzmann weight factorises into nearest-neighbour terms so $Z=\mathrm{Tr}\,T^N$; for large $N$ the largest eigenvalue dominates, $Z\approx\lambda_+^N$; so the free energy per spin is $-kT\ln\lambda_+$, and the ratio of eigenvalues gives the correlation length.
p7-l049-ising-model-transfer-matrix.modelAnswer: Each neighbouring pair contributes a factor $T_{ss'}$, so the sum over all spin configurations is $\mathrm{Tr}\,T^N$. For large $N$ the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_+$ dominates, giving $F/N=-kT\ln\lambda_+$, and the ratio $\lambda_-/\lambda_+$ sets the correlation length.

p7-l050-domain-walls-metropolis.prompt: Why does the one-dimensional Ising chain not order at any $T>0$?
options: Because the ordered state has higher energy than the disordered state at every temperature.
Because the chain is too short to have any interactions that could support long-range order.
Because the transfer matrix has a zero eigenvalue, which removes the possibility of a transition, which leaves no possible route to order at any temperature.
One domain wall costs $2J$ but has $\sim N$ positions, giving $k\ln N$ entropy; walls proliferate.
p7-l050-domain-walls-metropolis.explanation: In higher dimensions a domain wall costs energy proportional to its area, which grows with $N$ and beats the entropy gain.

p7-l050-domain-walls-metropolis.prompt: In a Metropolis Monte Carlo simulation of the 2D Ising model, what is the rule for accepting a trial spin flip with energy change $\Delta E$?
options: Accept if $\Delta E\le0$, else accept with probability $e^{-\Delta E/kT}$, sampling the Boltzmann weight.
Always accept flips that raise the energy, since raising the energy is what the heat bath does.
Accept only flips that lower the energy, since the system should always move toward equilibrium.
Accept all flips with probability one half, so that the spins reach a random configuration.
p7-l050-domain-walls-metropolis.explanation: The algorithm satisfies detailed balance, so long runs sample the canonical ensemble. Averages of $m$, $E$ etc. then estimate thermodynamic quantities.

p7-l050-domain-walls-metropolis.prompt: Explain the domain-wall argument for the absence of a phase transition in the one-dimensional Ising model, in your own words.
p7-l050-domain-walls-metropolis.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) in 1D flipping a whole block creates just two (or one) domain walls costing energy ~2J per wall; (2) the walls can be located at about N positions, giving entropy gain k ln N; (3) the free energy change 2J - kT ln N is negative for large N at any T>0, so order is destroyed.
p7-l050-domain-walls-metropolis.modelAnswer: Starting from the fully aligned state, flip half of the chain: this creates one domain wall at energy cost $2J$. The wall can sit at any of $N$ positions, so the entropy gain is $k\ln N$. The change in free energy $2J-kT\ln N$ becomes negative for large $N$ at any $T>0$, so such walls always appear and there is no long-range order.

p7-l051-mean-field-self-consistency.prompt: What approximation is made in the mean-field theory of the Ising model?
options: The interaction is switched off above $T_c$, so the spins behave independently there.
All spins are assumed independent of one another at every temperature, with no interaction at all.
Each spin feels the average magnetisation of its neighbours, ignoring their fluctuations and correlations.
The lattice is assumed infinite and every spin is assumed to point the same way from the start.
p7-l051-mean-field-self-consistency.explanation: Replacing $s_j$ by $\langle s\rangle=m$ gives an effective field $h+Jzm$. It ignores correlations between spin fluctuations.

p7-l051-mean-field-self-consistency.prompt: Just below $T_c$ mean-field theory predicts $m\propto(T_c-T)^{1/2}$. What does this tell you about the transition?
options: The magnetisation jumps discontinuously at $T_c$, as in a first-order transition.
The magnetisation grows linearly in $T_c-T$ just below $T_c$, with a finite slope.
The magnetisation is unchanged across $T_c$, so the transition is not visible in $m$.
The order parameter rises continuously from zero, with infinite slope: a second-order transition.
p7-l051-mean-field-self-consistency.explanation: Real 3D magnets have exponent about 0.33; exact 2D Ising has 1/8: the correlations that mean-field ignores matter near $T_c$.

p7-l051-mean-field-self-consistency.prompt: Estimate the mean-field critical temperature $T_c=zJ/k$ for a square-lattice ($z=4$) magnet with exchange coupling $J=1.0$ meV. Give it in K.
p7-l051-mean-field-self-consistency.explanation: $T_c=4\times1.0\text{ meV}/k=46.4$ K (the exact 2D result is lower, $2.27J/k=26$ K, because fluctuations suppress ordering).

p7-l051-mean-field-self-consistency.prompt: Derive the mean-field self-consistency equation $m=\tanh[\beta(Jzm+h)]$ for the Ising model.
p7-l051-mean-field-self-consistency.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) pick one spin, replace its z neighbours by their average m, giving effective field h_eff = h + J z m; (2) a spin in field h_eff has energy -h_eff s, so <s> = tanh(beta h_eff); (3) requiring <s> = m gives m = tanh[beta(h + J z m)].
p7-l051-mean-field-self-consistency.modelAnswer: Pick a spin; replace each of its $z$ neighbours by the average $m$. It then feels an effective field $h_{eff}=h+Jzm$ and has energy $-h_{eff}s$ with $s=\pm1$, so $\langle s\rangle=\tanh(\beta h_{eff})$. Self-consistency requires $\langle s\rangle=m$, giving $m=\tanh[\beta(Jzm+h)]$.

p7-l052-mean-field-free-energy-validity.prompt: Mean-field theory predicts a transition for the 1D Ising chain ($T_c=2J/k$) although the exact solution has none. In which situations is mean-field theory most reliable?
options: In low dimensions, where each spin has few neighbours and the average is easy to compute.
In high dimensions ($d\ge4$) or with long-range forces, where many neighbours average out fluctuations.
Only at $T=0$, where the spins are all aligned and the fluctuations are completely absent.
Only in one dimension, where the exact transfer-matrix solution agrees with the mean-field result, where the exact transfer-matrix solution agrees with the mean-field theory.
p7-l052-mean-field-free-energy-validity.explanation: More neighbours means the average field is a better approximation of the instantaneous field.

p7-l052-mean-field-free-energy-validity.prompt: In mean-field theory the heat capacity of an Ising magnet shows what behaviour at $T_c$?
options: A finite jump, because the magnetic energy vanishes continuously as $m^2\propto T_c-T$.
A divergence, because fluctuations become correlated over all length scales at $T_c$.
No anomaly at all, because the transition is continuous in the magnetisation.
A delta-function spike, because latent heat is released at the transition.
p7-l052-mean-field-free-energy-validity.explanation: With energy $\propto -m^2$ and $m^2\propto T_c-T$ below $T_c$, the slope $dU/dT$ changes abruptly, giving a jump (about $\tfrac32Nk$) rather than a divergence; real systems diverge or cusp because mean-field ignores fluctuations.

p7-l052-mean-field-free-energy-validity.prompt: Explain what mean-field theory neglects and why, as a result, it overestimates the tendency to order. Use the one-dimensional Ising chain, where mean-field gives $T_c=2J/k$ but the exact result is no transition, as an example.
p7-l052-mean-field-free-energy-validity.rubric: Full credit requires: each spin responds to the average field of its neighbours and fluctuations/correlations are neglected; fluctuations (domain walls) destroy order in low dimension; mean-field is more accurate with many neighbours (high $d$ or long range).
p7-l052-mean-field-free-energy-validity.modelAnswer: Mean-field replaces the neighbours of each spin with their average, ignoring fluctuations. In 1D, thermal domain walls destroy order at any $T>0$, but mean-field predicts $T_c=2J/k$. Its predictions improve as the number of neighbours grows, so fluctuations average out.

p7-l053-landau-theory-mean-field-exponen.prompt: In Landau theory the free energy is $F=F_0+a(T-T_c)m^2+bm^4$ with $a,b>0$. What is the equilibrium $m$ for $T>T_c$ and $T<T_c$?
options: $m=0$ at all temperatures, since the free energy has a single minimum for every $T$.
$m\neq0$ at all temperatures, since the quartic term always favours a finite magnetisation.
$m=0$ above $T_c$; below it $m=\pm\sqrt{a(T_c-T)/2b}$, growing continuously from zero.
$m$ jumps from zero to a finite value at $T_c$, since the free energy has two competing minima.
p7-l053-landau-theory-mean-field-exponen.explanation: Minimising gives $2a(T-T_c)m+4bm^3=0$. The sign change of the quadratic coefficient creates two symmetric minima.

p7-l053-landau-theory-mean-field-exponen.prompt: In mean-field theory the susceptibility diverges as $\chi\propto|T-T_c|^{-\gamma}$ with $\gamma=1$. By what factor is $\chi$ larger at $|T-T_c|/T_c=0.001$ than at $0.1$?
p7-l053-landau-theory-mean-field-exponen.explanation: A factor of $(0.1/0.001)^\gamma=100$ for $\gamma=1$. (With the true 3D Ising $\gamma=1.24$ it would be about 300.)

p7-l053-landau-theory-mean-field-exponen.prompt: Starting from the Landau free energy with $a(T-T_c)m^2+bm^4$, show that mean-field theory predicts $m\propto(T_c-T)^{1/2}$, i.e. the exponent $\beta=1/2$.
p7-l053-landau-theory-mean-field-exponen.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) set dF/dm = 0: 2a(T-T_c)m + 4 b m^3 = 0; (2) nonzero solution: m^2 = a(T_c-T)/(2b); (3) hence m proportional to (T_c - T)^(1/2) and beta = 1/2.
p7-l053-landau-theory-mean-field-exponen.modelAnswer: Minimising: $\partial F/\partial m=2a(T-T_c)m+4bm^3=0$. For $T<T_c$ the nonzero solution has $m^2=a(T_c-T)/2b$, so $m\propto(T_c-T)^{1/2}$ and $\beta=1/2$.

p7-l054-first-order-transitions-universa.prompt: What kind of term in the Landau free energy can produce a first-order transition?
options: A cubic term $cm^3$ (if symmetry allows), or a negative quartic term with a positive $m^6$ term.
Only a larger quadratic coefficient, which would move the transition to a higher temperature.
A purely quadratic term, since a single parabola can have two minima as the coefficient changes.
No terms can: Landau theory describes only second-order transitions, whatever terms are included.
p7-l054-first-order-transitions-universa.explanation: These produce a free-energy landscape with two competing minima, so $m$ jumps at the transition and there is latent heat.

p7-l054-first-order-transitions-universa.prompt: The liquid-gas critical point and the Ising magnet have the same critical exponents. What principle explains this?
options: Universality: exponents depend on dimension and order-parameter symmetry, not on microscopic details.
They are made of the same atoms, so that their critical behaviour is naturally identical.
It is an accident of the Ising model, which happens to match the liquid-gas data.
Exponents are always the mean-field values, whatever the system, so all systems agree.
p7-l054-first-order-transitions-universa.explanation: Near $T_c$ the correlation length is much larger than any microscopic scale, so microscopic details are irrelevant.

p7-l054-first-order-transitions-universa.prompt: Explain what universality means for critical phenomena, and why the liquid-gas critical point and the Ising ferromagnet share the same critical exponents even though their microscopic physics is very different.
p7-l054-first-order-transitions-universa.rubric: Full credit requires: exponents depend only on spatial dimension and the symmetry of the order parameter (and range of interactions), not on microscopic details; near $T_c$ the correlation length is much larger than the microscopic scale, so details wash out; liquid-gas density difference and Ising magnetisation are both scalar ($Z_2$) order parameters in 3D.
p7-l054-first-order-transitions-universa.modelAnswer: Near a critical point the correlation length greatly exceeds the molecular scale, so microscopic details wash out. Only dimension and order-parameter symmetry matter. The liquid-gas density difference and the Ising magnetisation are both one-component scalars in 3D, so they share an exponent set.

p7-l055-moments-cumulants-poisson-gaussi.prompt: The number of molecules in a small region of an ideal gas follows a Poisson distribution with mean 100. What is the standard deviation?
options: 100, since the standard deviation of a count equals its mean for a Poisson distribution.
10, because for a Poisson distribution the variance equals the mean.
1, since the count is an integer and can only differ from its mean by one unit.
50, since the standard deviation of a count is about half of its mean.
p7-l055-moments-cumulants-poisson-gaussi.explanation: Variance $=\bar N$, so relative fluctuation $1/\sqrt{\bar N}=10\%$. This is the origin of the visible 'graininess' of small samples.

p7-l055-moments-cumulants-poisson-gaussi.prompt: A volume of 1 mm$^3$ of air at standard conditions contains on average $2.69\times10^{16}$ molecules. Treating the number as Poisson distributed, what is the relative fluctuation $\sigma/\bar N$ in the number of molecules?
p7-l055-moments-cumulants-poisson-gaussi.explanation: $\sigma/\bar N=1/\sqrt{2.69\times10^{16}}=6.10e-09$, about six parts in a billion: invisible.

p7-l055-moments-cumulants-poisson-gaussi.prompt: Explain why the variance of a Poisson distribution equals its mean, and what this implies about the fluctuations of the number of molecules in a small volume of gas.
p7-l055-moments-cumulants-poisson-gaussi.rubric: Full credit requires: Poisson arises from many independent rare events (each molecule independently inside or outside the volume); variance = mean $=\bar N$; so relative fluctuation $=1/\sqrt{\bar N}$, large for few molecules and negligible for many.
p7-l055-moments-cumulants-poisson-gaussi.modelAnswer: Counts of independent, rare occurrences follow a Poisson law whose variance equals its mean, so $\sigma=\sqrt{\bar N}$. The relative fluctuation $1/\sqrt{\bar N}$ is large for a few molecules and tiny for a macroscopic number.

p7-l056-clt-and-ensemble-equivalence.prompt: Why do relative fluctuations of extensive quantities such as total energy scale as $1/\sqrt N$?
options: Because the individual contributions are perfectly correlated, so the fluctuations add up coherently.
Because the standard deviation is always proportional to the mean, whatever the size of the system.
The total is a sum of $N$ independent terms: its mean grows as $N$, its spread as $\sqrt N$.
Because larger systems have less energy per particle, so their fluctuations are proportionally smaller.
p7-l056-clt-and-ensemble-equivalence.explanation: Variances of independent contributions add: $\sigma^2=N\sigma_1^2$, so $\sigma/\mu\propto1/\sqrt N$.

p7-l056-clt-and-ensemble-equivalence.prompt: Why can we use the microcanonical or the canonical ensemble interchangeably for macroscopic systems?
options: Because energy is always exactly conserved in a heat bath, so the canonical energy does not vary.
Because the temperature does not matter in either ensemble, only the number of particles does.
Because the two ensembles are mathematically identical for any number of particles, large or small, so that fixed-$T$ and fixed-$E$ ensembles can never be told apart.
Canonical energy fluctuations are $\sim1/\sqrt N$, negligible for large $N$, so the two ensembles agree.
p7-l056-clt-and-ensemble-equivalence.explanation: Ensemble equivalence fails only for small systems or at critical points where fluctuations become large.

p7-l056-clt-and-ensemble-equivalence.prompt: State the central limit theorem and explain why it justifies thermodynamics as a deterministic theory of macroscopic systems.
p7-l056-clt-and-ensemble-equivalence.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the sum of many independent random variables with finite variance tends to a Gaussian, with mean N*mu and standard deviation sqrt(N)*sigma; (2) extensive quantities are such sums, so their relative fluctuations scale as 1/sqrt(N); (3) for N ~ 10^23 these are ~10^-12, so averages are sharply defined and thermodynamics is effectively deterministic.
p7-l056-clt-and-ensemble-equivalence.modelAnswer: The central limit theorem says that the sum of $N$ independent variables with finite variance is approximately Gaussian with mean $N\mu$ and standard deviation $\sqrt N\sigma$. Extensive thermodynamic quantities are such sums, so their relative fluctuations are $\sim1/\sqrt N\sim10^{-12}$ for $N\sim10^{23}$. Macroscopic quantities are therefore effectively sharp, which is why thermodynamics is deterministic.

p7-l057-microcanonical-and-canonical-ens.prompt: In the canonical ensemble the system's energy is not fixed. What does this imply?
options: The energy is exactly zero, as the bath absorbs any energy that the system may have.
The system cannot be described statistically, since its energy no longer has a definite value.
The temperature is fluctuating wildly, because the bath changes it from moment to moment.
The energy fluctuates about its mean by a relative amount $\sim1/\sqrt N$, negligible for large $N$.
p7-l057-microcanonical-and-canonical-ens.explanation: Thermal contact with a bath allows energy exchange; $T$ is fixed by the bath.

p7-l057-microcanonical-and-canonical-ens.prompt: Which thermodynamic potential follows directly from the canonical partition function $Z(T,V,N)$?
options: The Helmholtz free energy, $F=-kT\ln Z$.
The internal energy, $U=-kT\ln Z$.
The Gibbs free energy, $G=-kT\ln Z$.
The entropy, $S=k\ln Z$.
p7-l057-microcanonical-and-canonical-ens.explanation: The canonical ensemble has fixed $T,V,N$, whose natural potential is the Helmholtz free energy $F=-kT\ln Z$; $U$ and $S$ follow by differentiation.

p7-l057-microcanonical-and-canonical-ens.prompt: Describe how the canonical ensemble is obtained from the microcanonical ensemble by coupling the system to a heat bath.
p7-l057-microcanonical-and-canonical-ens.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the system plus bath is isolated and described by the microcanonical ensemble; (2) tracing over the bath, the probability of a system microstate with energy E_s is proportional to the number of bath states, which falls as exp(-E_s/kT); (3) so the system obeys the Boltzmann distribution with fixed temperature set by the bath.
p7-l057-microcanonical-and-canonical-ens.modelAnswer: System plus bath is isolated, so it is microcanonical with all joint microstates equally likely. The probability of a system microstate with energy $E_s$ is proportional to the number of bath microstates with energy $E-E_s$, which is $\propto e^{-E_s/kT}$ for a large bath. The system therefore follows the canonical (Boltzmann) distribution at the bath's temperature.

p7-l058-grand-canonical-and-choosing-ens.prompt: Which ensemble is appropriate for a small region of a gas that can exchange both energy and particles with the rest of the gas?
options: The microcanonical ensemble, since the region of gas has a definite energy at any given time.
The canonical ensemble, since the region exchanges heat with the rest of the gas around it.
The grand canonical ensemble, with fixed $T$ and $\mu$; energy and $N$ both fluctuate.
None of them can describe an open system, which needs a separate formalism altogether.
p7-l058-grand-canonical-and-choosing-ens.explanation: Microcanonical: isolated ($E,V,N$ fixed); canonical: heat bath ($T,V,N$); grand canonical: heat and particle bath ($T,V,\mu$).

p7-l058-grand-canonical-and-choosing-ens.prompt: What is the grand potential $\Phi=-kT\ln Z_G$ for a homogeneous system?
options: $\Phi=U-TS-\mu N=-PV$, the Legendre transform of $U$ in $S$ and $N$.
$\Phi=U+PV-TS$, which is the Gibbs free energy of a system at fixed $T$ and $P$.
$\Phi=TS$, the heat content of the system at the temperature of the bath.
$\Phi=U+PV$, which is the enthalpy of the system at fixed pressure.
p7-l058-grand-canonical-and-choosing-ens.explanation: It is the Legendre transform of $U$ with respect to $S$ and $N$; for a uniform system its extensivity gives $-PV$ (the Euler relation).

p7-l058-grand-canonical-and-choosing-ens.prompt: For 1.00 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K, the grand potential is $\Phi=-PV=-nRT$. Compute $\Phi$ in kJ.
p7-l058-grand-canonical-and-choosing-ens.explanation: $\Phi=-nRT=-2.494$ kJ; the magnitude equals the work $PV$ the gas does when it makes room for itself.

p7-l058-grand-canonical-and-choosing-ens.prompt: Explain how the grand canonical ensemble arises from the canonical one by letting the system exchange particles with a reservoir, and why $\Phi=-PV$ for a homogeneous system.
p7-l058-grand-canonical-and-choosing-ens.rubric: Full credit requires: the reservoir exchange adds the factor $e^{\mu N/kT}$ so $\mathcal Z=\sum_N e^{\mu N/kT}Z_N$; $\Phi=U-TS-\mu N$; Euler's relation $U=TS-PV+\mu N$ for an extensive homogeneous system gives $\Phi=-PV$.
p7-l058-grand-canonical-and-choosing-ens.modelAnswer: Allowing particle exchange weights each canonical sector $Z_N$ by $e^{\mu N/kT}$, giving $\mathcal Z$ and $\Phi=-kT\ln\mathcal Z=U-TS-\mu N$. For an extensive homogeneous system the Euler relation $U=TS-PV+\mu N$ then gives $\Phi=-PV$.

p7-l059-energy-fluctuations-fluctuation-.prompt: The relation $\mathrm{Var}(E)=kT^2C_V$ says what about heat capacity?
options: Heat capacity measures only the average energy of the system, not how it varies from moment to moment.
Large $C_V$ means large energy fluctuations: the response to $T$ is tied to spontaneous fluctuations.
Fluctuations are independent of the heat capacity, which is a bulk property of the material.
Fluctuations are smaller when the heat capacity is larger, since a large $C_V$ stabilises the energy.
p7-l059-energy-fluctuations-fluctuation-.explanation: This is a first example of the fluctuation-response (fluctuation-dissipation) idea: equilibrium fluctuations determine linear response coefficients.

p7-l059-energy-fluctuations-fluctuation-.prompt: Using $\mathrm{Var}(E)=kT^2C_V$ and $C_V=\tfrac32Nk$, estimate the relative energy fluctuation $\sigma_E/U$ for one mole of a monatomic ideal gas ($U=\tfrac32NkT$).
p7-l059-energy-fluctuations-fluctuation-.explanation: $\sigma_E/U=\sqrt{2/(3N)}=1.05e-12$: about $10^{-12}$, so the energy is sharp to a part in a trillion.

p7-l059-energy-fluctuations-fluctuation-.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) <E> = -d ln Z / d beta and <E^2> = (1/Z) d^2 Z / d beta^2; (2) Var(E) = d^2 ln Z / d beta^2 = -d<E>/d beta; (3) since d/d beta = -kT^2 d/dT, this equals kT^2 dU/dT = kT^2 C_V.
p7-l059-energy-fluctuations-fluctuation-.modelAnswer: $\langle E\rangle=-\partial_\beta\ln Z$ and $\langle E^2\rangle=Z^{-1}\partial_\beta^2Z$. Then $\mathrm{Var}(E)=\partial_\beta^2\ln Z=-\partial_\beta\langle E\rangle$. Since $\partial_\beta=-kT^2\partial_T$, $\mathrm{Var}(E)=kT^2\,\partial U/\partial T=kT^2C_V$.

p7-l060-number-fluctuations-critical-opa.prompt: Near the liquid-gas critical point, a transparent fluid becomes milky. What is the cause of this critical opalescence?
options: The fluid becomes a solid, and the crystals scatter light in all directions.
Compressibility diverges, so density fluctuations on the scale of light's wavelength scatter strongly.
The fluid decomposes chemically near the critical point, forming a colloid of fine particles.
The temperature suddenly drops, and the cold fluid condenses into a fog of droplets.
p7-l060-number-fluctuations-critical-opa.explanation: Number fluctuations are related to compressibility: $\langle\Delta N^2\rangle/\langle N\rangle=nkT\kappa_T$. At the critical point $\kappa_T\to\infty$.

p7-l060-number-fluctuations-critical-opa.prompt: In the grand canonical ensemble, an ideal gas has $\langle\Delta N^2\rangle=\langle N\rangle$. What does this say?
options: The number of particles is exactly fixed, so no fluctuation in $N$ is possible at all.
The variance in $N$ is zero, so the gas has a perfectly sharp particle number.
The fluctuations of an ideal gas are larger than those of any real gas, because it has no interactions.
The number fluctuations are Poissonian, with relative size $1/\sqrt{\langle N\rangle}$.
p7-l060-number-fluctuations-critical-opa.explanation: Interactions increase or decrease fluctuations (via the compressibility), but an ideal gas gives exactly the Poisson value.

p7-l060-number-fluctuations-critical-opa.prompt: Explain why the size of number (density) fluctuations in the grand canonical ensemble is controlled by the compressibility, and what happens to both at a liquid-gas critical point.
p7-l060-number-fluctuations-critical-opa.rubric: Full credit requires: $\langle\Delta N^2\rangle\propto kT(\partial N/\partial\mu)\propto\kappa_T$; a compressible system lets particles move in or out of a region at little free-energy cost; at the critical point $\kappa_T\to\infty$ so fluctuations grow over all scales, causing strong light scattering (critical opalescence).
p7-l060-number-fluctuations-critical-opa.modelAnswer: The variance of $N$ is $kT(\partial N/\partial\mu)$, proportional to the isothermal compressibility: when little pressure change is needed to alter the density, density fluctuations are large. At a critical point $\kappa_T$ diverges, so fluctuations on the scale of light's wavelength scatter light strongly.

p7-l061-classical-partition-function-clu.prompt: Why does the classical partition function of an interacting gas contain the factors $1/N!$ and $1/h^{3N}$?
options: $1/N!$ for indistinguishable particles; $h^{3N}$ makes the phase-space integral a count of quantum states.
They arise from the interaction potential, which sets the weight given to each configuration.
Both come from the equipartition theorem, which fixes the weight of each phase-space cell.
They are arbitrary constants with no effect on observables, which could be set to any value.
p7-l061-classical-partition-function-clu.explanation: The $h^{3N}$ is irrelevant for energy and pressure but needed for absolute entropy (it fixes the constant in Sackur-Tetrode).

p7-l061-classical-partition-function-clu.prompt: In the cluster expansion, what is the Mayer function $f(r)=e^{-u(r)/kT}-1$ for a hard-core repulsion (potential infinite inside a diameter $d$)?
options: $f=-1$ inside the core, since the Boltzmann factor is zero there.
$f=0$ inside the core, since particles never overlap.
$f=+1$ inside the core, since the potential is infinite there.
$f=\infty$ inside the core, since $u\to\infty$ there.
p7-l061-classical-partition-function-clu.explanation: For $u=\infty$ the Boltzmann factor $e^{-u/kT}=0$, so $f=-1$ inside the core and $f=0$ outside where $u=0$. This excluded volume gives $B_2=\tfrac23\pi d^3$.

p7-l061-classical-partition-function-clu.prompt: Explain how the second virial coefficient emerges from the cluster expansion of the classical partition function, and what role the Mayer function plays.
p7-l061-classical-partition-function-clu.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) write Boltzmann factor of interaction as product of (1 + f_ij) with Mayer function f = e^{-U/kT} - 1, which is zero when particles are far apart; (2) expanding in powers of f groups terms by clusters of interacting particles; the leading correction involves pairs; (3) the pair term gives B2 = -(1/2) integral f(r) d^3r.
p7-l061-classical-partition-function-clu.modelAnswer: The interaction Boltzmann factor $e^{-\beta U}=\prod_{i<j}(1+f_{ij})$ with $f_{ij}=e^{-\beta u(r_{ij})}-1$, which vanishes for widely separated molecules. Expanding the product groups the terms by clusters; the lowest-order term involves isolated pairs, and integrating it gives the second virial coefficient $B_2=-\tfrac12\int f(r)\,d^3r$.

p7-l062-debye-huckel-limits-of-classical.prompt: A salt is added to a solution, increasing its ionic strength $I$. How does the Debye screening length $\lambda_D\propto I^{-1/2}$ change, and what does this mean for the potential around an ion?
options: It lengthens, so that the electrostatic potential of an ion reaches farther into the solution.
It is unchanged, since screening depends on the charge of the ion and not on the ionic strength.
It shortens: the ion cloud screens the central charge better, so the potential decays faster than $1/r$.
It becomes infinite, since the added salt cancels the charge of the central ion completely.
p7-l062-debye-huckel-limits-of-classical.explanation: Debye-Hückel: $\phi(r)=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon r}e^{-r/\lambda_D}$. More ions means a smaller $\lambda_D$, which affects activity coefficients in solution chemistry.

p7-l062-debye-huckel-limits-of-classical.prompt: Classical statistical mechanics predicts that every molecular rotation and vibration contributes $\tfrac12kT$ per quadratic term at all temperatures. Where does this fail?
options: It fails only for noble gases, which have no rotational or vibrational degrees of freedom.
It fails at high temperature when particles move too fast, because relativistic effects then matter.
It never fails, since classical mechanics is exact for molecules at every temperature.
It fails when $kT$ is below a mode's level spacing, e.g. H$_2$ rotation below about 85 K.
p7-l062-debye-huckel-limits-of-classical.explanation: Classical results are the high-temperature limit of the quantum partition function.

p7-l062-debye-huckel-limits-of-classical.prompt: The Debye screening length for a 1:1 electrolyte in water at 25 $^\circ$C is $\lambda_D=\sqrt{\epsilon_r\epsilon_0kT/(2N_Ae^2I)}$ with ionic strength $I$ in mol/m$^3$. For $I=0.100$ mol/L (100 mol/m$^3$) and $\epsilon_r=78.5$, find $\lambda_D$ in nm.
p7-l062-debye-huckel-limits-of-classical.explanation: $\lambda_D=0.96$ nm, a few ion diameters. At $I=0.001$ M it would be 9.6 nm.

p7-l062-debye-huckel-limits-of-classical.prompt: Explain physically why an ion in an electrolyte is surrounded by a cloud of counter-ions, and how the thickness of this cloud depends on the ionic strength.
p7-l062-debye-huckel-limits-of-classical.rubric: Full credit requires: opposite charges are attracted and like charges repelled, with thermal motion competing; the net cloud screens the central charge, so the potential decays as $e^{-r/\lambda_D}/r$; $\lambda_D\propto I^{-1/2}$, so higher ionic strength gives a thinner cloud.
p7-l062-debye-huckel-limits-of-classical.modelAnswer: Counter-ions are attracted and co-ions repelled, while thermal motion spreads them out, forming a screening cloud. The potential decays as $e^{-r/\lambda_D}/r$ with $\lambda_D\propto I^{-1/2}$, so adding salt compresses the cloud.
